title: WhatsApp Voice-Note Superintendent for Spec Builders
one_liner: A bilingual coordinator-plus-AI service that runs daily crew confirmations, headcounts and re-sequencing for a builder's two dozen subs over WhatsApp voice notes, priced per house.
customer: Small private and spec builders (20-300 homes a year) in Texas, Florida and the Southeast, and remodelers who juggle many subs.
problem: A typical home needs about two dozen subs. Foundations sit 30+ days waiting for crews, and one executive described 15-20 houses stuck 6+ weeks. Builders learn a crew is not coming days too late. Project software requires English typing and logins, and workers are wary of anything that looks like tracking. Procore's 20 agents serve larger GCs.
solution: Foremen keep sending Spanish voice notes on WhatsApp. The system transcribes them, extracts headcount, phase status and photos, and updates the schedule. A nearshore bilingual coordinator confirms tomorrow's crews by 5 p.m., calls backup crews when there is a gap, and sends the builder one exception report each morning. Privacy by design: counts and progress only, no IDs or location.
why_now: ICE arrests rose from 32,545 in May to 49,571 in July 2026. Crews can shrink overnight (a Minnesota roofing crew went from 80 to 6). Multilingual speech models and the WhatsApp Business API are mature, and PM incumbents are focused on big GCs.
revenue_model: $300-500 per active house per month, or $3-6K per month per builder. One coordinator handles 25-40 houses, so gross margin is high.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not scheduling math, it is that the people who know whether tomorrow's crew is coming do not use the software. The interface must be the phone and language they already use. The daily headcount is the leading indicator, and knowing a day earlier lets a builder re-sequence trades instead of idling a foundation.
first_30_days: Sign 3 builders with 10-20 active houses each through a home builders association. Hire one bilingual coordinator. Run it manually with WhatsApp and a shared sheet, add speech-to-text in week 2, and document five saved crew-days.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Hyphen Solutions (BuildPro / SupplyPro), Procore (Daily Log Agent and 4 other AI agents), Fieldwire (Hilti), Trunk Tools (TrunkText). White space: Research coverage was thin. The WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was exhausted before my searches ran, so I had no search results at all. I did not use WebFetch as a search-engine workaround, and instead fetched about a dozen specific vendor and reference pages directly. Buildertrend returned 403 and NAHB's labor page returned 404. I did NOT check Crunchbase, YC, TechCrunch, Product Hunt or GitHub, so I could not confirm whether any startup already sells WhatsApp voice-note crew confirmation. On the pages I did fetch, no company combines all of the following: (1) WhatsApp voice notes as the only interface for foremen, with no app or login; (2) Spanish-first speech transcription of headcount and phase status; (3) a human bilingual coordinator who confirms next-day crews by 5 p.m. and calls backup crews; (4) a morning exception report to the builder; (5) per-house pricing aimed at 20-300 home/yr spec builders. Vendors on the market are either app-and-login tools (Procore, Fieldwire, Raken, JobTread, BuildTools), large-GC AI (Trunk Tools, Procore agents), civil crew dispatch (Assignar), or production-builder infrastructure (Hyphen). The unserved slice is the mid-size spec builder, where the foreman's phone and language is the system of record and the deliverable is a confirmed crew rather than software. It is unserved partly because it is a labor-arbitrage service business that VC-backed software companies avoid.

title: Payoff-Triggered Refund Recovery for Credit Unions
one_liner: A payoff-desk plug-in that finds the unearned GAP and service-contract refunds the moment a member pays off, and applies unearned add-on credits in repossession deficiencies. It goes through lenders, not SEO, so it reaches the borrowers the consumer refund sites can't.
customer: Credit unions and regional auto lenders (payoff and collections departments). The lender pays a small SaaS fee or takes a share of recovered money. Second wedge: consumer bankruptcy and debt-defense attorneys and legal aid, at $99 per deficiency audit.
problem: When a borrower pays off early, trades in, or has the car totaled or repossessed, they are owed the unearned pro-rata part of GAP, service contracts and other financed add-ons. Refunds are not automatic. Not the dealer, not the lender and not the administrator processes them, and consumer-refund sites exist because so few people claim. The incentives point the wrong way. The dealer suffers a commission chargeback, so it stalls. The administrator profits from non-cancellation. The lender never owned the product. The borrower doesn't know. In repossession, unearned add-on credits should reduce the deficiency the borrower is sued for, and they rarely appear on deficiency notices. Roughly 3M repossessions a year and subprime 60+ day delinquency at a 32-year record of 6.9% in January 2026 make this a very large pool of missed money.
solution: Ingest the closed-loan document image or loan tape, read the itemized products and financed amounts from the retail installment contract, and match each to its administrator. Compute the pro-rata or earned-basis refund by state rule (New Jersey, for example, requires an automatic refund within 60 days). Auto-generate the cancellation packet with the lender's payoff letter, odometer statement, signature or letter of authority, and the state statute citation, then track it to payment. Stalled cases escalate to the state insurance department with a complaint file. The moat is a database of roughly 60 administrators' actual cancellation requirements and response behavior, plus the 50-state rule set. The repossession product reconciles deficiency notices against the same data and outputs an attorney-ready exhibit.
why_now: Record delinquencies and about 3M repossessions a year, roughly 84-month loans with about 30% of trade-ins underwater, and long terms mean most loans die early and carry stacked add-ons. Credit unions are under member-experience and fee-optics pressure, and California's SB 766 now requires dealers to keep refund and cancellation records. LLMs can finally read messy contract images and cancellation forms cheaply enough to run at scale.
revenue_model: Credit union pays $3 to $6 per payoff processed, or 20 to 30% of recovered money with no upfront fee. Attorneys pay $99 per deficiency audit or a $499 per month subscription. Later, sell aggregated administrator refund-speed benchmarks to dealer groups and regulators.
non_obvious_insight: The consumer refund sites that exist all have the same weakness: they wait for the borrower to show up. The one moment every party knows the loan ended is the payoff, and the lender's payoff desk is the only place that sees all of them. The refund itself comes from the administrator's pool, and the dealer's chargeback is a fight between the dealer and the administrator. The borrower's claim doesn't depend on the dealer cooperating, so the dealer stalling does not need to hold up the refund.
first_30_days: Build the administrator playbook for the 20 largest GAP and service-contract administrators and the 10 highest-population states. Offer 3 credit unions a free retrospective audit of 500 payoffs from the last 12 months and show them the dollar total of unclaimed refunds. Take a 30% success fee on live recoveries. Simultaneously give 5 consumer bankruptcy attorneys the repossession deficiency audit free on their next 3 cases in return for case studies.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Origence (formerly CU Direct) - loan origination/indirect platform (CUDL), Assurant (F&I administrator and TPA), Unverified: consumer GAP/VSC refund-claim services (contingency), Unverified: in-house lender recovery and collections teams and BPO vendors. White space: Verification was limited. The WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was exhausted before I could run any queries, and only about 15 direct URL fetches were possible, many of which 404'd or were blocked. That leaves three points.

1. I found no direct competitor selling a payoff-triggered GAP/VSC refund plug-in to credit unions. Origence, the dominant CU indirect-lending platform, and Assurant, a major administrator, show no such product on their homepages.

2. Genuinely unserved and specific, if the market read holds:
   - A per-payoff, lender-integrated refund workflow for dealer-sold, financed add-ons at credit unions.
   - A 50-state pro-rata rules engine combined with an administrator-by-administrator cancellation-requirements database.
   - An attorney-ready audit of repossession deficiency notices that reconciles unearned add-on credits. Consumer-bankruptcy and debt-defense attorneys and legal aid are plausible buyers, because the lender's or dealer's incentive runs against the borrower.

3. Weaknesses in the idea as written, from reasoning rather than found evidence:
   - The claim that the lender never owned the product is shaky. Under many state retail installment sales acts, and under the FTC Holder Rule, the assignee or holder can carry refund and credit obligations. That helps demand, as a compliance and UDAAP driver, but it changes the pitch from 'find hidden money' to 'reduce liability'.
   - A 20-30% success fee taken from a member's own refund has poor fee optics for a credit union. It also conflicts with the idea's own member-experience rationale.
   - On payoff, the refund goes to the borrower, so the CU gets no direct economic benefit. The CU's incentive is goodwill and compliance, not revenue.
   - CU vendor due diligence and core/LOS integration will make the sales cycle slow.
   - The California SB 766 citation in the idea did not check out. The leginfo summary I fetched for the 2023-24 bill described an unrelated social-worker licensing bill. Do not rely on that cite until it is confirmed.

title: Commissioning Passport: The Data Center Readiness Standard
one_liner: Invert the model: the sponsor pays a neutral party to verify hall readiness once, in a machine-readable ledger every lender, insurer, landlord and offtaker can read, which grows into the standard definition of ready-for-service and the trigger written into loan, lease and backstop documents.
customer: Payers: sub-investment-grade neocloud sponsors and colocation developers, who face 4-6 counterparties each re-diligencing the same hall (issuer-pays). Readers who license access: lenders, DSU insurers, offtakers and backstop providers. Supply side, seeded free: commissioning agents, general contractors and IEs, who become named attestors.
problem: One liquid-cooled hall is diligenced repeatedly. The GPU-loan lender, the landlord's lender, the DSU insurer, the offtaker and any GPU-vendor backstop provider each hire their own advisor or IE, and evidence moves as emailed PDFs. Sponsors lose days on every draw and every counterparty re-asks the same questions. There is no shared definition of 'ready for service'. Lease commencement, financial close and backstop triggers can each key off a different milestone, and a backstop can lapse if construction runs more than about 180 days late. Because credibility is scarce, sponsors post letters of credit or parent guarantees, which is expensive capital to lock up.
solution: Two things. First, an open 'Readiness Ladder' spec, about 40 evidence-backed binary milestones for the last 90 days, published free so it can be adopted like a template. Second, the Passport ledger. Evidence is captured at source (Cx platform exports, utility letters, OEM startup bookings, CDU flush certificates, gear serial and bill-of-lading matches), timestamped and hashed, and tied to a named attestor (Cx agent, IE, OEM technician, utility). We add independent spot audits and a per-party permissioned view. Outputs are a Passport Score, a probability of RFS by date using reference-class priors, and a covenant schedule template (for example 'Ladder milestone L-7 certified in Passport') that counsel can drop into loan, lease and backstop documents so RFS is defined once. First product, sellable within 6 months, is the 'Draw Pack': within 5 business days of a draw or tranche request, we convert the sponsor's own commissioning evidence into a verified Passport snapshot that the lender has agreed to accept. It costs the sponsor $15K per pack or $8K/month per hall. Pilots go to sponsors that lenders cap, for whom verified readiness is a currency. The capture workspace is free for Cx agents and GCs, which seeds the supply side.
why_now: Lenders are capping neocloud exposure, deals are stalling on credit and some operators demand letters of credit or parent backing. Multi-party GPU structures with vendor backstops mean the same hall gets underwritten by many parties at once. The first-principles cost stack changed: turning IST results, punch lists and flush logs into structured pass/fail facts used to take a 3-person review team, and document AI now makes one reviewer per hall economically feasible. That makes portable verify-once evidence cheap enough to sell to the party that would otherwise pay for every counterparty's separate review. It would not have worked in 2019, when there was no GPU-debt market and no extraction tooling.
revenue_model: Issuer-pays verification at $15K per pack or $8-12K/month per hall. Read-side seats for lenders, insurers and offtakers at $40-150K per year, free for the first year to any lender that writes the Ladder into its documents. Licensed Passport Score and delivery-time benchmark indices for funds and reinsurers. Later, lenders offer margin step-downs or lower letter-of-credit haircuts for Passport-verified halls, and we take a fee from the sponsor's saving. Scale illustration: 150 halls under continuous verification at about $100K per year blended is about $15M revenue, with data licensing on top.
non_obvious_insight: Verification is a public good with a payer problem, and the answer is the one project-finance already uses. IEs are borrower-paid but lender-selected, and rating agencies are issuer-paid. The independence safeguards are a lender-vetoable attestor panel, published methodology and an audit trail. For the sponsor the product sells speed and a cheaper substitute for letters of credit and parent guarantees, not virtue. The moat is a cornered dataset: durations by OEM, utility, GC and hall type across every verified hall, which makes forecasts better as more halls join, so the network effect is in the prior. Counter-positioning also works: incumbents bill by the hour for each counterparty, and a portable verify-once artifact cannibalizes that repeat billing. The standard is won by whoever gets its definition of RFS into the legal templates first.
first_30_days: Publish Ladder spec v0.1 and teardowns of 2 publicly delayed projects, built from public documents. Recruit 4 Cx leads and one finance lawyer to draft the covenant schedule. Interview 15 sponsors and 10 lenders to measure which draw-package friction costs the most days and dollars. Sign 2 design partners: one sub-IG neocloud sponsor with a live delayed-draw facility, and its lender, who agrees in writing to accept the pack. Run the service by hand ('Wizard of Oz'): shared drive, spreadsheet and document-AI extraction, with no product build yet. Success by day 45: one lender accepts a Passport pack in place of a second-round advisor visit. Riskiest assumption to test first: sponsors will pay for verification that lenders accept, and lenders will accept sponsor-paid attestation. If not, fall back to Offspring 1 (lender-paid) and keep the ledger as a by-product.
lineage: mutation of I0365 ('Ground-Truth Diligence for GPU-Backed Lenders'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SynMax Vulcan (with Industrial Info Resources data partnership), Currence (formerly Sightline Climate), Epoch AI Frontier Data Centers Hub, SemiAnalysis (consulting, AI Datacenter Model, ClusterMAX). White space: The unserved wedge is narrow but real. (1) No product found in this session combines a binary, evidence-backed 'Readiness Ladder' for the last 90 days before RFS (utility energization letter, MV gear energization, Cx Level 4/5 and IST pass/fail counts, CDU flush and pressure tests, fiber acceptance, punch-list burn-down, OEM startup-tech availability) with a probabilistic RFS-by-date output and draw or covenant triggers. (2) Satellite and database vendors (SynMax, IIR, Currence, Epoch) cover the exterior and the announced schedule, and their materials do not claim commissioning or energization evidence. (3) GPU-deal technical advisors, as described by Peony, focus on fleet, telemetry and power documents rather than data hall commissioning. (4) Traditional IEs are slow, tied to a single lender or borrower, and priced for large project-finance deals. A fixed-fee, two-week, desk-plus-site 'second opinion' for a private credit desk, insurer or offtaker appears unserved. (5) The offtaker and backstop side (AI labs signing take-or-pay capacity, Google or Nvidia-style backstop providers) is structurally underserved because IEs work for lenders. Risks: incumbent IEs and Cx firms can add this as a service line, SemiAnalysis could bolt it on, and the business is people-bound (bench of ex-Cx leads) with limited software moat. Access to sites, contractors and Cx records depends on borrower cooperation, which means lender-imposed information covenants or offtaker leverage. | How this version avoids them: Traditional IEs (Sargent & Lundy markets data center commissioning oversight and lender due diligence, so they are real incumbents): the Passport makes them attestors and partners, so they are a supply-side channel, not a rival. This also blunts the incumbent-adds-a-service-line risk, because their work becomes an input to our ledger. SynMax/IIR, Epoch, Currence: exterior and desk data, taken as inputs and potential co-marketing or referral partners. SemiAnalysis: paid research and ratings-style brands for neocloud operations, not hall-level evidence, and possibly a distribution partner for the index. Peony: a data-room vendor for fleet and telemetry files that could add a Cx module, so it is the closest emerging rival to watch, or an integration partner. Uptime Tier: a one-time end-of-build certificate on design and performance, not a continuous last-90-days schedule ledger. Risks I could not verify: whether lenders will accept issuer-paid evidence, and whether an established engineering firm would launch a competing 'portable' standard once the concept is visible. Publishing the spec early and embedding it in legal templates is the defense.

title: Recorder Rails: County-Funded Clean Index of Instruments
one_liner: AI re-indexing and compliance scans that counties buy from their own records-modernization funds. In return we hold the cleaned, entity-resolved index of every non-deed instrument, which becomes the data layer for assembly alerts and much else.
customer: County recorders and clerks (about 3,100 counties), who pay first, starting with mid-size rural and exurban counties in data-center and energy corridors where economic development offices also want the assembly view. Downstream buyers are the parent's developers, utilities and funds, plus ag lenders and title-adjacent firms.
problem: The parent's product depends on county-by-county recorder access and on document types that are often wrong ('Other', 'Miscellaneous', 'Agreement'). Ingestion is a grind, bulk commercial-use rules vary, and the good data is scattered. Counties have their own pains: aging archives, mandated redaction of sensitive data, covenant-review requests and property-fraud pressure, all with thin staff. They already spend on indexing and digitization from earmarked funds. Nobody owns a clean cross-county index of non-deed instruments.
solution:
1. Sell the county a fixed-price Hidden Instruments Audit. AI reclassifies its mislabeled and 'Other' instruments from the images, corrects grantor and grantee indexing, flags sensitive-data and statutory items such as discriminatory covenants, and gives the county a corrected index and an economic-development view of large instruments.
2. In the agreement, the county gives bulk access to the images and index at cost, and we keep the right to publish the derived classification and entity graph. The underlying records are already public.
3. Publish an open taxonomy for non-deed instruments, in the manner of MISMO for mortgages, so counties and vendors can adopt it.
4. Keep the labeled corpus and the LLC-family graph proprietary and build products on it: Courthouse Tape alerts, the utility site-control check, landowner tools, alt-data licences and collateral-encumbrance alerts for ag lenders.
why_now: LLM vision has collapsed the cost of reading a scanned page, so a re-index that once cost a labor-intensive vendor per-page fees is now cheap. Counties are under fresh mandates to review archives: covenant-removal laws in a number of states, and reportedly some large counties have already run AI covenant scans (verify which). Property-fraud concern is high. FinCEN's exemption of domestic companies from beneficial-ownership reporting makes primary-record entity resolution more valuable. The large-load land rush gives the resulting index an immediate paying use. Rural counties facing data center proposals want visibility into assembly.
revenue_model: County audits at $9k-$40k per county, fitted under small-purchase thresholds and paid from records-modernization or technology funds, then $5k-$20k a year to maintain. Data licences to funds at $50k-$150k a year. Downstream product revenue per the parent: developer or utility seats at $2k-$8k a month and title packets at $750-$2,000. A plausible year-three target is 300 counties at about $25k, or $7.5M, plus $5M-$10M of licences and subscriptions. Gross margin on data products should exceed 70% once ingestion is standardized.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource is county cooperation, not the classifier. So invert who pays. Instead of buying access from counties, we get paid by them to solve a problem they already fund, and the by-product is the corpus. A county that gets a corrected index and a free economic-development dashboard has little reason to block a downstream data feed, and other counties will copy the arrangement. This is a cornered resource plus switching costs that build county by county. Incumbents face asymmetry: indexing and digitization vendors earn from labor-based per-page work, so AI re-indexing at a fraction of the price undercuts their own revenue. Title plants index for title, not for cross-county assembly detection.
first_30_days: Run an offline proof on two rumored-project counties. Pull 24 months of instruments, reclassify 'Other' and 'Agreement' filings, and count how many option memoranda were recorded before the announcement. If that count is low, shift the wedge to easement and transmission detection. Show each recorder the result: 'We found N large instruments mislabeled as Other.' Offer a $9,500 audit to three counties, and separately sell the free 'who is assembling where' memo to 10 site-selection consultants to fund the corpus. Check each state's rules on commercial use of bulk records and on data-sharing agreements, and get county counsel comfortable.
lineage: mutation of I0773 ('Courthouse Tape: Land-Assembly Radar for Infrastructure'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ATTOM Data, Reonomy, Regrid, Enverus. White space: The specific product in the idea, a feed that reads recorded option memoranda, leases and easements from county recorders, classifies them from the image rather than the clerk's label, clusters LLC families by notary, return-to firm and address, and alerts on assembly patterns, was not found at any vendor I could read. Everything I could read is adjacent. Parcel and ownership vendors (Regrid, ATTOM, Reonomy) sell deeds, mortgages and LLC piercing but not options or easements. Siting and diligence vendors (Paces, Enverus, GridCARE) help a client find its own site. Project trackers (Cleanview, DC Byte, Heatmap Pro, Data Center Watch) start at permit or public news. Land-management vendors (Pandell, Enverus LandScape) manage a client's own documents. What remains open is cross-county, image-level reading of recorded non-deed instruments to detect other parties' assembly, sold as alerts. It is plausibly protected by the hard part, which is getting recorder access county by county, not the ML. The main structural doubts I could not test are whether developers actually record option memoranda before announcement, and how many counties allow bulk commercial pulls of document images. | How this version avoids them: The parent's competitors are adjacent data sellers: ATTOM, Regrid and Reonomy sell deeds, mortgages and parcels; Enverus, Paces and GridCARE serve a client's own site; Cleanview, DC Byte and Heatmap Pro start after permits or news; Pandell manages a client's own documents. None of them controls the recorder relationship. Title plants such as First American DataTree hold indexed documents for title workflows, not a cleaned cross-county alert feed. The county-software and digitization vendors (Tyler, Fidlar and Kofile appear to be the main ones, none verified here) are the real risk and might build the same thing. We differ by working on top of whichever system the county runs, by contracting with the county rather than the vendor, and by owning the entity graph. Enverus can add a feature but not a hundred county contracts.

title: Owner-Side Ordering: The Royalty Asymmetry Calculator
one_liner: An advice-only LINE tool that tells franchise convenience-store owners how many fresh items to order and when to mark them down, using the owner's own payoff instead of HQ's.
customer: Franchise convenience-store owners in Japan, especially the many multi-store owners (roughly 55,000 stores nationally, all three chains). They pay a monthly fee plus a share of the waste they cut. First targets are Osaka owners reachable through the franchisee union and owner LINE groups.
problem: The royalty is charged on gross profit calculated as if discarded food never existed. At Seven, HQ absorbs only 15% of disposal cost and the owner absorbs 85%. So HQ's ordering AI and the field counselors (OFC) push order quantities toward what maximizes HQ's royalty, not the owner's take-home. Take a rice ball that costs ¥100 and sells at ¥160. With a 60% royalty on the ¥60 gross profit, the owner keeps about ¥24 when it sells and loses about ¥85 when it is binned. HQ makes about ¥36 on a sale and loses about ¥15 on a discard. The owner-optimal stocking level is far lower than HQ's, and no owner has a tool that shows this. Markdowns would close much of the gap, but staff are reluctant to apply stickers and owners fear the OFC's disapproval.
solution: The owner photographs the daily disposal-scan printout and the hourly sales sheet, or forwards a CSV. The tool never touches HQ systems. Each afternoon it returns a per-category order guide such as 'cut salmon onigiri by 4 at the 16:00 delivery, add 2 tempura udon'. It also gives a markdown clock, for example 'sticker at 20:40, deeper cut at 23:10', calculated from the owner's actual royalty tier, disposal share and sell-through curve. A one-page 'why I ordered less' printout gives the owner data to answer the OFC. Phase two adds an owner-side dashboard showing true hourly wage after royalty and self-labor. It also adds a contract-exit and renegotiation calculator, and anonymized peer benchmarks that owners can use collectively.
why_now: Osaka's minimum wage rises to ¥1,231 on 1 October 2026, up ¥54 after ¥63 last year. Labor is the biggest cost, and waste is the last controllable line item. HQ-side AI ordering is now the default, so owners increasingly follow machine suggestions they cannot audit. Chains have grudgingly allowed markdowns since the JFTC's 2009 order against Seven-Eleven Japan for obstructing them, but owners still lack tools to price them properly.
revenue_model: ¥4,900 per store per month, plus 20-25% of documented waste reduction for the first 12 months. If a store saves ¥80-100k a month, the fee is easy to justify. Multi-store owners get a bundle. Later revenue comes from an owner-benchmark subscription and referrals to specialist franchise lawyers and accountants.
non_obvious_insight: Waste is not a shared problem between HQ and owner. The contract makes it the owner's problem alone, while HQ's revenue is almost indifferent to it. The newsvendor critical ratio for the owner is about 22%, versus about 70% for HQ. Every 'AI ordering recommendation' is optimized for the wrong party's payoff. Nobody built the owner's-side calculator because owners fear retaliation and VCs assume HQ systems are neutral.
first_30_days: Use my three stores as the lab. Photograph two weeks of disposal sheets and hourly sales, then back-test the newsvendor plus markdown model against what actually happened. Build a LINE bot with photo OCR and a spreadsheet engine. Recruit 10 owners from union chat groups and Facebook franchisee groups. Run a free 4-week gain-share pilot with a signed baseline for each store. Publish a one-page 'royalty asymmetry' explainer that spreads owner-to-owner. Convert the pilot to paid at week 5.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Seven-Eleven Japan AI ordering plus HQ-led markdown (Eco da Ne), Lawson AI.CO (ordering plus AI markdown recommendation), FamilyMart AI Recommend Ordering, Sinops (sinops-CLOUD AI markdown) with Sato. White space: No product found that is an independent owner-side payoff engine for Japanese convenience-store franchisees. Searches in Japanese and English returned no startup, SaaS or app that (a) uses the owner's actual royalty tier and disposal-share contract terms to compute order levels, (b) sets markdown timing from the owner's payoff, or (c) audits HQ AI recommendations against the owner's interest. HQ tools (Seven, Lawson, FamilyMart) cover order and markdown outputs but are HQ-controlled and aimed at waste or sales, not owner take-home. Supermarket AI-markdown vendors (Sinops/Sato, Wasteless) sell to retailers, not franchisees. The union and ex-OFC consultants give advice with no calculators or automation. The unserved wedge is: HQ says X, your own contract math says Y, the yen difference is Z, plus contract-aware multi-store economics. Caveats: (1) Seven-Eleven's new contract (announced June 2026, effective autumn 2027) raises HQ's disposal-loss share from 15% to 50% (with a cap), lowers charge to 53%/67%, applies only to newly opened stores with no conversion planned for existing stores (https://www.ryutsuu.biz/strategy/s061915.html, https://www.watch.impress.co.jp/docs/news/2118977.html). At 50/50 the owner critical ratio rises from about 22% to roughly 36%, so the asymmetry mostly fades on new-contract stores but persists on legacy stores for years. (2) Seven's HQ-led markdown push since 2024 partly commoditizes the markdown clock. (3) The 22% vs 70% math checks out for the 85/15 split, but contract terms differ by chain (Lawson subsidy formula is more complex, FamilyMart is about 15%), so each chain needs its own model. (4) Franchise-agreement limits on data use and third-party tools were not verified.

title: Auto Loan-End Event Exchange for Add-On Refunds
one_liner: Start by recovering unearned add-on refunds on repossessed and charged-off loans for small lenders on pure contingency (cash the lender itself keeps), then turn those lender-attested loan-end events into a neutral exchange that administrators, carriers and regulators plug into, so refunds become a statutory event pushed to the administrator instead of a claim the borrower must pull.
customer: Stage 1: collections and recovery managers at credit unions and community banks with $200M to $3B in auto loans (too small for in-house recovery teams), plus the collection agencies and recovery BPOs that serve them. Stage 2 payers: GAP and service-contract administrators and their fronting or contractual-liability carriers and reinsurers; regulators get free access. Governance: founding lenders receive equity or rebates through a cooperative structure such as a CUSO.
problem: At repossession or charge-off, the unearned refund on financed GAP, service contracts and other add-ons is collectible cash for the lender and shrinks the deficiency billed to the member. Small lenders rarely chase it because each administrator has its own paper process and the dealer chargeback fight breeds stalling. The deeper failure is informational: where a state requires automatic refunds on payoff (the parent cites New Jersey; verify), the administrator cannot comply because nobody tells it the loan ended. No one sits between the lender who knows and the administrator who owes, so every refund is a bilateral fight with no shared standard, no SLA and no scoreboard.
solution: Stage 1, sellable within 6 months, is a Repo Refund Desk. The lender drops a monthly file of repossessions and charge-offs plus contract images (secure upload, no core integration). The system reads the add-ons, matches administrators, computes refunds by state rule, files cancellations under the lender's assignment of unearned premiums, and tracks to payment. Refunds post to the lender's loan account, cutting both the write-off and the member's deficiency. Fee: 20 to 25% of cash actually recovered, nothing upfront. title: Graduate Pay Ledger for CDL Schools and Carriers
one_liner: CDL schools get the verified placement and earnings evidence Workforce Pell requires by having graduates upload settlement stubs to a pay-verification app. Carriers pay to reach those graduates with verified pay pages, and lenders pay for stub-based income packets.
customer: Small and mid-size CDL schools and other short-program providers (paying per completer verified) as the beachhead. Carriers with 50-1,000 trucks that pay $6-15k to hire a driver (verified-pay badge and graduate funnel), mortgage and auto lenders serving drivers, and state workforce boards.
problem: Workforce Pell requires verified placement (about 70%) with a clock that starts before the governor application, and CDL schools typically track completion, not employment. State wage records lag by quarters and miss owner-operators and per-diem pay. Meanwhile the pay-verification app has a cold-start problem: recruiting drivers one Facebook group at a time is slow and noisy.
solution: At completion, schools enroll graduates in the pay app. In exchange for a verified profile and a small incentive, graduates upload their first settlement stubs at 30, 90 and 180 days. The AI extracts employer, paid miles, deadhead, detention and pay per hour away from home. The school gets an audit-ready placement and earnings ledger, the governor application packet, and an earnings-premium exposure score. Carriers that look good buy a Verified Pay page and a graduate applicant funnel, and lenders buy income packets built from stubs.
why_now: Workforce Pell went live for provider approvals in 2026 and the placement and completion evidence rules make this a compliance purchase with a deadline. The stub-parsing AI is cheap now. Carriers are paying up to $15k per driver hired and are locked out of trust because drivers only believe stubs.
revenue_model: $150-300 per completer verified or $4-12k per year per program. $3-5k for a governor application packet. $1.5-3k earnings-premium exposure report. $500-3,000 per month carrier subscriptions for verified pay pages and graduate funnel. $300-1,000 lender referral fees per funded loan. title: Camp-Road Closing Rescue Plus Resale Toll
one_liner: A Maine-only, attorney-supervised service that runs the statutory neighbor meeting, records an enforceable assessment-lien covenant, and then issues a paid road-status letter on every future sale on that road.

The payer at the table is the seller, or the buyer via negotiated credit. Out-of-state second-home buyers and their lenders are the ones who insist on a maintenance agreement. Listing agents are a secondary channel in the Oct-Feb off-season, when they prep camps for spring listing.
problem: Maine Title 23 section 3101 (text re-checked today) lets as few as 3 parcels petition a notary to call a meeting, lets a majority vote set assessments, and shields board members from civil liability. It contains no lien or collection remedy. The parent research counted 4 parcels, but the fetched text says 3 parcels held by 3 different owners. So the statute is a vote without teeth, and nobody runs the vote. No closing attorney will chase 14 owners for proxies at a flat closing fee, so the sale stalls or closes on a handshake. The parent's own flaws sit on top of this. Its $12-25 per household per month is 6 to 12 times PayHOA's price anchor. Holding dues float triggers trust-account rules. A 5-8% procurement fee is a conflict of interest. Its plan to have attorneys send deals for a flat fee is a RESPA Section 8 trap, because 12 CFR 1024.14 bars referral fees and unearned fees in federally related mortgage transactions and permits payment only for services actually performed.
solution: Sell 'Meeting-in-a-Box' as a fixed-scope, attorney-supervised package. We do the non-billable grunt work: map benefiting parcels from the registry of deeds and county GIS, serve statutory notice, run the notary-called meeting (in person plus absentee and proxy ballots), keep minutes, collect the officer slate and a treasurer, take a baseline road-condition photo log, and handle recording. The supervising attorney, either the closing attorney or our contracted Maine counsel, owns the legal instrument: a recorded covenant that adds what the statute lacks (assessment lien running with the land, successor obligation, reserve requirement, estoppel-letter mechanism). We build no dues software and hold no money. Each association opens a bank account with a treasurer, and we hand over a checklist plus a PayHOA or plain-ACH setup guide. After formation we run one annual notice-and-meeting cycle and issue a road-status letter (dues current, no open assessments, maintenance agreement on record) whenever a house on the road sells. This works like the HOA resale certificate. No referral fees are paid to anyone. Attorneys bill their own legal work, and our fee is a disclosed third-party service line.
why_now: Maine's statute already exists, so formation is process work rather than a legal breakthrough. Post-2020 in-migration put many out-of-state buyers on camp roads they do not understand. Housing turnover is historically low (roughly 3-4% a year, an assumption to confirm), so every stalled closing costs a seller and an agent real money. Hurricane Helene's NC private-road program showed that aid and repair money flow only to an organized counterparty with a named contact, which makes 'pre-formed association' a sellable feature. Oct-Feb is slack season for Maine camp closings, so attorneys have time to try a new workflow before spring listings. Cheap document automation and e-signature make proxy and absentee ballot logistics a small cost rather than a paralegal week.
revenue_model: Formation: $1,400 flat per road, paid at closing from seller proceeds or by the neighborhood, disclosed as a third-party service. Attorney legal review is billed separately by the attorney at roughly $300-500. Recurring: $200 per association per year, flat rather than per household, for annual notice, meeting, officer changes and records. Transaction toll: $175 per road-status letter, paid by the seller at each future sale. With about 9 coordinator hours plus recording fees per formation, gross margin should be near 60-65%. Rough year-1 target is 40 roads, or about $56k formation plus $8k recurring. At 300 roads with about 18 homes each and 3-4% turnover, resale letters add about $35k a year. That makes a real but modest Maine business, and the scalable asset is the state-by-state playbook plus the registry.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing in Maine is not the entity, since the statute lets neighbors make one, and not the legal template, which is a commodity. It is the person who runs the meeting and the recorded covenant that gives assessments teeth. The first closing buys the association, and every later closing pays a toll, so a formed road becomes a perpetual, transaction-priced revenue stream. That toll avoids the PayHOA per-household price anchor and sits where the money is, in seller proceeds. Because the attorney does the legal work under supervision and is never paid to refer, the attorney channel is RESPA-clean and the attorney stops being the substitute. Over time title agents learn to ask for our letter, which creates switching costs because the association's officer and records live with us.
first_30_days: Week 1: retain a Maine real estate attorney on a flat $3-5k engagement to draft the covenant with lien language, the estoppel-letter form and the meeting script. Have that attorney confirm the lien is enforceable when drafted as a recorded covenant and confirm the RESPA-safe fee structure. Weeks 1-3: hold 20 calls with lakes-region and midcoast closing attorneys and title agents and ask which of their last 12 months' closings hit a road issue, what happened, and what they would pay to have it handled. Weeks 2-4: run 2 pilot roads (one tied to a live or stalled closing) at a $600 pilot price, and measure owner participation rate, days to majority vote, and hours per road. By day 30, get 3 firms to sign a one-page agreement to route their next road problem to us at $1,400. The riskiest assumption to kill early is whether attorneys will buy outsourced meeting logistics rather than absorb it.

title: Deficiency-Suit Add-On Credit Audits for Consumer Defense Firms
one_liner: A flat-fee, 24-hour audit that rebuilds a repossession deficiency from the retail installment contract and shows the unearned add-on credits, notice defects and fee errors the lender or debt buyer left out, sold to the consumer-defense lawyers who already have the client and the deadline.
customer: Consumer-defense and debt-defense attorneys and legal aid offices that defend post-repossession deficiency suits. Start in two or three states chosen from docket data in week 1 (candidates: Maryland, Pennsylvania, Ohio, where notice rules and fee-shifting tend to favor borrowers; confirm before committing). Wedge buyer: small consumer-law firms of 1 to 10 lawyers that take flat-fee or fee-shifting cases, plus 3 to 5 legal aid units.
problem: A repossessed borrower is typically sued 6 to 18 months later, often by a debt buyer, on a one-line balance backed by a thin affidavit. The defense lawyer has about 30 days to answer, no numbers person, and a flat fee or grant-funded hours. The deficiency figure usually does not credit the unearned GAP, service-contract and other add-ons that were rolled into the loan, and may carry defective post-sale notices or inflated fees. Rebuilding it by hand takes a paralegal hours, so most defendants default or settle blind. The parent's borrower-side value is real but lacked a buyer with standing, a deadline and a fee-shifting statute. This buyer has all three.
solution: The attorney uploads the complaint, contract image, pre- and post-sale notices and auction bill. Within 24 hours the tool returns a Deficiency Autopsy PDF: (1) a rebuilt ledger from the retail installment contract (amount financed, itemized add-ons, finance charge, payments, fees); (2) unearned add-on credits owed under the contract and state rule, with the administrator's cancellation requirement and a computed pro-rata figure; (3) a notice checklist against UCC Article 9 and the state motor-vehicle finance act (timing, required content, explanation of the deficiency calculation, commercial-reasonableness red flags such as sale price versus wholesale value, and whether a defective notice bars the deficiency in that state); (4) an exposure sheet covering offsets, defenses and potential statutory damages under UCC 9-625(c)(2) as adopted by the state; (5) draft answer paragraphs, counterclaim language and targeted discovery requests aimed at cancellation records. A human analyst reviews every output at first, later only exceptions. Flat fee only, never a share of a fee award, which avoids fee-sharing problems with non-lawyers (Rule 5.4) and keeps this an attorney work tool rather than advice to consumers.
why_now: Subprime 60+ day delinquency hit a 32-year high in January 2026 and roughly 3M repossessions a year feed a deficiency pipeline that debt buyers monetize through suits. 84-month loans and underwater trade-ins make deficiencies large, so a $99 audit is small next to the dollars at stake per case. LLMs now read messy contract scans, auction bills and notices for cents per case, which was not economic in 2022. Federal consumer-finance enforcement has retrenched since 2025 (verify), so what enforcement remains is private and state-level, and it runs through exactly these lawyers.
revenue_model: $99 per audit; $499 per month for up to 8 audits plus template library for small firms; about $2,400 per year site licenses for legal aid; $750 for attorney-directed analyst declarations. Second, higher-value stream: anonymized pattern reports on defect prevalence by lender, debt buyer and collection law firm (for example, the share of one plaintiff's notices that omit add-on credits), sold to class-action firms and state AG staff at $25K to $100K per report. Audit revenue alone is a small wedge (likely single-digit millions a year), so the dataset and pattern reports are the scale path.
non_obvious_insight: Each audit is a product and a labeled data point. Deficiency defects are systematic because one plaintiff's template produces the same omission in every case, and UCC 9-625 statutory damages attach per consumer, so the pattern is worth far more to class counsel than a single case is to a defendant. The parent's flaw, that lender incentives run against the borrower, becomes the moat: lenders and their in-house recovery teams can never sell this because they are the party being audited. The borrower's claim also needs a number and a deadline, not the dealer's or administrator's cooperation.
first_30_days: Week 1: pull about 300 recent deficiency complaints from public dockets in the candidate states (plaintiff, amount, whether the defendant had counsel) to pick two states and list the 10 heaviest filers; have a consumer-law ethics lawyer review the template for unauthorized-practice and fee-sharing risk. Weeks 2 to 3: ask 15 consumer-defense firms and 3 legal aid units (through NACA, NCLC and state consumer-law listservs) for their next 3 deficiency cases free in return for a written outcome; deliver each audit manually in 24 hours using LLM extraction plus an analyst. Week 4: switch to $99, publish an anonymized 'five places deficiency numbers lie' guide, and log the dollar swing on every case. Target: 30 audits delivered, 10 paid, 5 documented cases where the balance moved by more than $1,000.

title: Payable Bias Audit for Black Mass Sellers
one_liner: A fixed-price audit that measures, in euros per year, the systematic sampling bias between a black mass seller's protocol and its buyer's. The fix is then locked in as a sealed sample-of-record and a two-line contract clause.
customer: Wedge: independent mechanical pre-processors and EV/ESS dismantlers in Germany, Poland and Benelux. They sell roughly 300-3,000 t/yr of black mass (about EUR 1-8M/yr) to one or two hydromet buyers on a binding buyer-gate assay. About 40-60 such sellers exist in the corridor. The buyer of the audit is the owner, CFO or commercial director who signs the offtake contract, not the QA chemist. Gigafactory scrap desks come later, since they have in-house metallurgists and slow procurement.
problem: The parent sells noise reduction, but random sampling noise mostly nets out for a seller shipping 40-100 lots a year. What does not net out is systematic bias between two protocols. A grab from the top of a big bag or drum, an unrecorded moisture basis, and segregation of coarse Cu/Al foil against fine cathode powder all push in one direction on every lot, so bias moves money one way. A 3% payable bias on EUR 5M of annual sales is EUR 150k a year, invisible lot by lot. The umpire clause cannot catch it. Bureau Veritas's own umpire page (fetched this session) describes umpire work as its own analysis of samples, that is, a re-assay of the retained sample. If the retained sample carries the bias, the umpire confirms it. Sellers therefore concede, or split the difference, on lots they were systematically shorted on.
solution: Step 0 costs nothing. Ask the seller for 30-plus historical lots with its own dispatch assay and the buyer's settlement assay. A significant one-signed mean gap qualifies the prospect. It might be lab bias or sampling bias, and the audit separates the two. Step 1 is the Paired-Protocol Bias Audit, sold at EUR 20-30k. Over 8-10 lots, take three samples per lot: the seller's method, the buyer's documented method, and a Theory-of-Sampling incremental sample from a falling stream or drum auger, split by rotary divider into sealed triplicates. Blind full-digestion assays go to one accredited lab, with a 20% cross-check at a second. The deliverable is the bias with a confidence interval, the euros per year it costs, a Gy heterogeneity and sampling-variance statement, and a written seller Sampling Protocol of Record. Step 2 is a per-lot Sample-of-Record service using a portable kit of about EUR 15-25k (rotary divider, riffle splitters, balance, drying oven, inert glove bag). It gives sealed triplicates at load-out and a two-line clause: 'sample of record taken per Protocol v1, sampling variance not to exceed x% relative at 95%, retained split binds on dispute'. If the buyer refuses the clause, the seller holds the data to shop the volume to another recycler. No containerised station is built until an anchor customer pays for one.
why_now: Several Western recyclers restructured or were bought out in 2025 (Li-Cycle into Glencore, per the parent research), so sellers are already renegotiating counterparty terms and a new clause is on the table anyway. Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/606 has been in force since 24 July 2025, and recyclers report annually to member-state authorities from 2026. Composition data for intermediate fractions such as black mass therefore has to be documented, which turns a written sampling protocol into a compliance artefact. Ni/Co price swings make each percentage point of payable worth more.
revenue_model: Audit fee of EUR 20-30k, with about EUR 10-12k of lab pass-through. Per-lot Sample-of-Record fee of EUR 900-1,800, or EUR 8-15 per tonne. Optional protocol licence to a buyer who wants to adopt the seller's protocol as its own. Year-1 target: 6 audits and 4 conversions at about 40 lots each, roughly EUR 350-400k revenue on about EUR 40k of kit. It is deliberately a small service business first, and the dataset of bias by protocol is the asset it builds.
non_obvious_insight: The value is the sign and size of the bias, not the reduction in variance. The party it costs is the natural buyer, and it is already identifiable from settlement history before any sampling. That makes the sales motion outbound and quantified (euros lost per year) instead of a vague accuracy pitch. A 'no bias found' result is also sellable, as a clean bill for lenders and counterparties. Because the umpire re-assays the same retained sample, no incumbent product is structured to detect the effect.
first_30_days: Week 1: retain a named senior sampling practitioner and an accredited partner lab. Anchor Protocol v1 to representative-sampling standards such as DS 3077 and, by analogy, ISO 12743 for concentrates. Both are recalled from memory, so verify. Build a one-page leak calculator from public payables and the seller's own settlement pairs. Weeks 2-3: send it to 40 named sellers in the DE/PL corridor and run the historical-pair test for every taker. Weeks 3-4: sign three audits at cost (about EUR 12k of pass-through each) in return for permission to publish anonymised results. Buy or lease a used rotary divider and portable kit. Go/no-go: at least 2 of 3 show a bias worth more than the audit fee, otherwise pivot to offspring 2 or 3.

title: Tariff Surcharge Clawback for B2B Buyers
one_liner: A contingency-fee service that mines a buyer's 2025-26 supplier invoices for 'tariff surcharge' lines and recovers a share of the IEEPA refunds those suppliers are now collecting.
customer: Multi-unit restaurant and retail franchisees, contractor purchasing co-ops, and mid-market distributors' customers that paid itemized tariff, freight or 'inflation' surcharges to suppliers who were the importer of record. They pay a 20-30% success fee on money recovered.
problem: IEEPA duty refunds go only to the importer of record (IOR) or a party the IOR designates. Buyers who paid the tariff as a surcharge or a higher price get nothing unless they ask. AutoZone booked about $96M and Cracker Barrel $15M, with MillerKnoll $16.5M and Worthington $4M. Downstream buyers have no visibility into what their suppliers recovered and no process to ask for it.
solution: Read-only inbox and AP connectors pull 2025-26 invoices and extract surcharge, 'tariff', 'duty' and 'trade cost recovery' line items. The system estimates each supplier's IEEPA exposure from public import-manifest data. It checks the supplier's terms for pass-back language, such as 'surcharge will be removed or refunded if tariffs are rescinded'. It then generates a claim letter with an offer to accept credit memos or to have the supplier name the buyer as the CBP Form 4811 notify party so the refund routes to the buyer. A second module audits new diesel and fuel surcharges against the contract formula and the EIA diesel index. Claims are sent to the top 20 suppliers per buyer, and unclaimed money is tracked to closure.
why_now: CBP's CAPE portal opened in 2026 and is issuing refunds within 60-90 days of an accepted declaration. Refunds are landing in Q3-Q4 2026 P&Ls as one-time gains. Suppliers are least defensible in the first months after booking a windfall and will negotiate to keep customer goodwill. Diesel is $6.53/gal, up $2.78 year over year, so a wave of fresh surcharge invoices is arriving that nobody audits.
revenue_model: A 20-30% contingency fee on recovered refunds and credits, plus $199-$999/month for continuous surcharge auditing (fuel, energy, 'regulatory recovery' fees) once the first recovery lands.
non_obvious_insight: The refund windfall is a transfer from customers to importers, and the CFOs say so. AutoZone's CFO said 'the refund environment was deflationary, and the industry likely would have raised prices faster if both retailers and suppliers hadn't received cost relief' (https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/22/autozone-azo-q4-2026-earnings-call-transcript/). Cracker Barrel booked a $15M refund and MillerKnoll $16.5M, worth 180 bps of gross margin (https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/23/cracker-barrel-cbrl-q4-2026-earnings-call-transcript/ and https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/22/mlkn-q1-2027-earnings-call-transcript/). CBP states 'Only the IOR ... or the authorized customs broker ... may file' and never mentions downstream buyers, couriers or DDP shipments (https://www.cbp.gov/trade/programs-administration/trade-remedies/ieepa-duty-refunds). Every downstream claim is therefore a negotiation, and the buyer who holds the 2025 invoices has the leverage. Nobody is selling that to the buyer side. The legal caveat is that the buyer needs an explicit surcharge line or contract language to have a real claim, so the product should target only those cases.
first_30_days: Recruit 5-8 restaurant franchisee groups or contractor purchasing co-ops through franchisee associations and buying-group managers, with a free 'we only get paid if you get paid' offer. Export 2025 AP data or forward invoice PDFs, then have an analyst plus an LLM extraction script build a surcharge ledger for the top 15 suppliers each. Send the first 30 claim letters with a one-page template that cites the refund program and asks for credit or 4811 routing. Have a supply-chain lawyer review the template. Aim to close the first paid recovery within 60-75 days.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: TariffRefund, PRGX (recovery audit / AP profit recovery), Cass Information Systems (freight audit and payment), AFS Logistics (freight audit, parcel audit, post-audit). White space: Provisional: I found no product or startup that mines a buyer's supplier invoices for tariff surcharge lines and pursues the supplier for a share of the IEEPA refund, on the buyer's behalf and for a contingency fee. The importer side is being served (TariffRefund.com self-serve, plus customs brokers and consultants). Freight and parcel audit vendors cover surcharge auditing. Generic AP recovery audit (PRGX) is the closest capability. What looks unserved is the buyer-as-claimant workflow: an automated surcharge ledger, supplier IEEPA-exposure estimates, contract pass-back language checks, claim letters, and CBP Form 4811 notify-party routing. It would target mid-market multi-unit franchisees, buying co-ops and GPOs, who are too small for PRGX-style enterprise engagements. The fuel-surcharge module is NOT white space because freight audit is a mature, crowded category. Caveat: my competitor scan is incomplete. The web-search budget was exhausted before any search ran, so this rests on direct page fetches of the CBP page, earnings transcripts and a handful of guessed vendor sites. Law-firm class actions or demand-letter campaigns, tariff-refund startups I could not surface, and customs brokers or couriers adding a pass-through service were not checked.

title: Neutral Registry and Standard for Neighbor Baselines
one_liner: An independent, vendor-agnostic registry and open protocol that notarizes pre-construction baselines from any sensor vendor or consultant, gets referenced in county ordinances and a model presumption statute, and becomes the title-plant-style record that insurers and lenders underwrite against.
customer: Three payers, sequenced. (1) Sensor vendors and developer-hired consultancies (KETOS, Aethair, Kunak resellers, TRC and Salas O'Brien-type firms) that need a neutral stamp so counties will believe their data. (2) Data center developers who must file a baseline to satisfy an ordinance or a hearing (50-500 MW campuses in contested counties). (3) Later, insurers, lenders and state agencies buying registry data and certification. Counties and regulators are the standard's adopters, not payers.
problem: Every county and agency is inventing its own baseline rules: a 48-hour ambient sound survey here, monitoring wells and a hydrogeologist there (Franklin County IN, Chadds Ford PA, Shenandoah VA, St. Louis, Virginia DEQ's five Kunak sensors in Loudoun). Developer-hired consultants produce the data, so residents distrust it; opposition-side groups produce competing data, so developers distrust that. Nothing makes a baseline tamper-evident, comparable across sites, or legally meaningful. Unlike Pennsylvania's Act 13 for oil and gas (operators pay for pre-drill tests, and a rebuttable presumption applies when no baseline exists), no data-center equivalent creates a legal reason to buy, which is the parent's biggest unproven assumption.
solution: Build the audit-firm layer for baselines, in four steps. (1) Protocol v1, open and free: sensor siting rules, control-site design, QA/QC, minimum 90 days pre-application, chain of custody and data schema for wells, noise, PM2.5 and voltage, written with a land-grant university hydrogeologist and an acoustician. (2) The registry: any vendor submits raw data through an API, and we run automated QA, protocol audit and dual-key custody (a university library or state geological survey as second custodian, plus RFC 3161-style public timestamp logs, no token). The output is a Registered Baseline certificate with tamper-evident, first-in timestamps and a public read-only view. (3) The adoption engine: a one-page ordinance rider ('baseline must be registered under an independent public-benefit protocol') sent to every county drafting rules, and a model bill for the January 2027 legislative sessions (TX and NY are the pressure points) that adapts the Act 13 logic: a registered baseline lets a developer rebut unsupported claims, while no registered baseline shifts the presumption to the operator. (4) Governance: a public-benefit board with county, university, developer and resident seats, so no vendor controls it. Year 2-3 balance-sheet option: once 30+ campuses are registered, use the loss-relevant data to launch a developer-owned risk retention group or mutual for neighbor-harm guarantees, with the registry as its underwriting file. The same registry then extends to other large-load neighbors (battery storage, fabs, lithium, hydrogen).
why_now: The moratorium wave (NY EO 62 on July 14, Texas TCEQ halt on Sept 21, local pauses) means regulators must define 'what evidence counts' before lifting pauses. State legislatures convene in January 2027. Counties are copy-pasting bespoke baseline language right now, so an early standard can be the copied text. Public-sector baselines are starting (Virginia DEQ's Loudoun air sensors since Feb 2026) and need tamper-evident custody, and the Newton County lawsuit (Sept 2026) is a live example of dueling studies. Sensor prices collapsed, so the scarce input is now trust, not data.
revenue_model: Registry filing fee of $15-25k per site (protocol audit, QA, dual-key custody, certificate) plus $3-6k per year custody for 10 years; vendor and assessor certification of about $10k per firm per year for the registry-verified listing; data and API licences to insurers, lenders, state agencies and researchers; later, a premium share if a mutual launches. Bottom-up sketch: 150 new registrations per year at $20k = $3M; 500 custodied sites at $4.5k = $2.25M; 60 certified firms at $10k = $0.6M; about $6M per year by year 3 from data centers alone, with the upside from adjacent industries and underwriting data. Sales-cycle proxy: a filing is a line item in a permit budget, not a new budget.
non_obvious_insight: The incumbents are the channel, not the enemy. Developer-hired consultants and sensor vendors already produce the baselines but cannot be believed, and their best sales asset is a credible neutral attestation, exactly as companies prepare their own books but need an independent auditor to be trusted. So the registry sells to the competitors' customers through the competitors, and vendors pay to be certified because counties will ask for it. The moat is a cornered resource (first-in timestamped pre-construction baselines cannot be recreated after a site is built), network economies (cross-site data improves control models and expected-loss estimates) and switching costs (10-year custody), backed by counter-positioning (a vendor cannot be neutral without giving up its own product). The lever that decides everything is the legal presumption, which is why the model bill and ordinance rider are part of the product, not lobbying on the side.
first_30_days: Days 1-14: draft Protocol v0.1 with a land-grant extension hydrogeologist and an independent acoustician; publish it CC-BY with a one-page ordinance rider. Days 10-25: send the rider to the county attorneys behind Franklin County IN, Shenandoah VA, Chadds Ford PA and 10 other counties with open drafts; ask to be named as an acceptable registry. Days 15-30: sign 3-5 letters of intent from sensor vendors and consultancies to submit pilot baselines for the Registered Baseline certificate; book calls with two state association-of-counties or legislative staff on presumption language for TX and NY. Sell the first two filings ($12-18k pilot pricing) to developers with hearings in the next 60-90 days. Six-month target: 10 registered sites, 3 vendors certified, one ordinance or permit condition naming the registry, $150-250k of fees. Gate: if no county or regulator will reference the protocol within 6 months, fall back to selling attestations as a service inside the well-trustee model (offspring 1).
lineage: mutation of I1172 ('Neutral Baselines and Neighbor Guarantees for Data Centers'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: KETOS (SHIELD / KELP data-center water monitoring), Aethair (Aethair PRO, Environet, Thiamis), Envirosuite (ASX:EVS), Kunak. White space: Nobody found sells the bundle, so the status is 'gap' and not 'open'. The sensor and baseline layer is not open: KETOS (about $45M raised) pitches an independent baseline for data centers, Aethair pitches pre-construction baselines, Envirosuite has community dashboards, and consultancies bundle baselines into permitting. The unserved wedge is what sits on top of the sensors. (1) A neutral administrator holding escrowed, tamper-evident data whose governance the county and community accept, unlike developer-hired consultants and unlike opposition-side groups such as CEDS. (2) The Neighbor Guarantee: an automatic, no-litigation payout to households from a developer-funded escrow when a pre-agreed trigger is hit. No vendor, insurer, county ordinance or developer program found does this. The nearest things are Franklin County, Indiana's draft rule (escrow for 24-hour emergency potable water to impacted neighbors, plus developer-funded monitoring wells), one-off buyouts and lump-sum checks. (3) A 10-year, multi-parameter (wells, noise, PM2.5, voltage) record packaged as a permit-condition template that regulators can adopt. Weak points: the sensor baseline will commoditize; attribution is hard, because well drawdown from drought or other pumping is indistinguishable from data-center drawdown unless the design uses upgradient control wells and pumping records; automatic payouts may look like insurance under state law; and developer counsel may resist a pre-committed payout as an admission of liability. Note: the web-search budget ran out before I could check Crunchbase/YC directly for a startup doing exactly the escrow-plus-parametric bundle, so 'nobody found' means no evidence in about 25 searches, not proof of absence. | How this version avoids them: It does not compete with KETOS, Aethair, Kunak, Clarity, Larson Davis or Eno on hardware or dashboards; they submit data and pay to be verified, so their marketing (KETOS's 'missing baseline', Aethair's pre-construction guide) creates our demand. Envirosuite, the strongest incumbent, sells recurring monitoring SaaS to sites that pay it and cannot credibly be the independent notary of its own customers' data. Consultancies (TRC, Salas O'Brien, Trinity, SCS) are developer-hired and gain from a stamp that makes their work believed. CEDS advises opposition groups and is not neutral, but its recommended pre-, during- and post-construction baselines match our protocol, so it is a natural endorser. Prevolt and Jambo sell engagement and risk screens, not evidence custody. Developer substitutes (checks, buyouts, pledges) are unrelated budgets. No standard-setting registry for data-center baselines surfaced in the parent's research or in a fresh search of ordinances and guidance, which showed bespoke county-by-county language.

title: Cattle Lien Registry and Sale-Barn Exit Alerts
one_liner: Invert the problem: instead of counting cattle in the pasture, watch the few gates cattle must leave through. Start with consignment alerts to lenders and lien matching for auction markets, then grow into the neutral title registry for cattle.
customer: Two-sided. Lenders with cattle collateral pay first. Livestock auction markets, which carry conversion liability when they sell pledged cattle without paying the lienholder, supply the data and pay later. Wedge: one region where 8-12 markets and 10-20 lenders overlap (for example the Nebraska Sandhills, Flint Hills or northern plains), so alerts are dense enough to matter. Eventual customers are feedyards, packers, brand agencies, participation buyers and secondary-market programs.
problem: Cattle have no VIN or title. A lender's lien follows the animals to sale, but the barn's lien check is a paper or fax list of seller names plus state central-filing lists. Borrowers consign under a relative's name, a shell entity or a barn 150 miles away, and the lender finds out months later at the next inspection, or never. Markets are exposed to conversion suits and often end up paying twice, once to the seller's account and once to the lender. Counting cattle on inspection day cannot catch cattle sold the day after, or the same cattle pledged twice (the parent's fraud case, claimed and unverified, involved a $2.8M loan against 850 head).
solution: Phase 1 (sellable in 6 months), 'Consignment Alert'. The lender uploads a pledged-collateral profile per loan: legal entities, DBAs, family names, brands, counties and any tag or EID lists from chute scans or borrower spreadsheets. Markets email or upload their consignment list before sale day, as they already assemble it for clerks. Fuzzy matching on name, brand, county and tag produces an alert to the lender ('Borrower X consigned 143 steers at Y Thursday') and a prompt to the market to issue a joint-payee check. Phase 2: EID matching. Chute-side scans (the parent's product) and barn intake scans feed the registry, so alerts match animals, not just names. Phase 3: the registry becomes a title layer where pledges and releases are recorded per animal or lot and queried by feedyards, packers, brand agencies and participation buyers. Verified movement history plus pledge status then supports collateral-managed advances on bred heifers (through a licensed lending or warehouse-funded partner) as the balance-sheet extension. The registry is tag-vendor-neutral and works on visual tags and brands where EID coverage is thin.
why_now: October-November is the peak fall calf run, so a pilot sees dense consignments right now, and lender annual renewals arrive in December-February. Digital EID tags are more common after the Nov 2024 federal rule. Cheap fuzzy entity matching and LLM parsing of messy consignment sheets make a small-team registry feasible where it was not in 2019. Record cattle prices and debt-financed herd rebuilding raise the dollars at risk per lien. A fresh fraud case (claimed in the parent, unverified) is making lenders ask what happens after the inspection. The neutral registry position is open until a tag vendor or state agency takes it.
revenue_model: Lenders pay $25-50/month per monitored loan ($300-600/yr). A bank with 150 loans is $45-90K/yr, and 40 banks is roughly $2-3M recurring. Markets get free lien checks at first because they are the data supply, then a $200-500/month tier for clearance workflow (joint-check prompts, an audit trail for their liability insurer). Later a per-lot clearance fee of $0.10-0.25/head consigned, on the well over 10M head a year that pass through auctions. Phase 3 adds registry-lookup fees from packers, feedyards and participation buyers, and net interest or fee share from collateral-managed advances through a licensed partner.
non_obvious_insight: Fraud needs an exit. Herds can be hidden, borrowed for inspection day or double-counted, but cattle converted to cash pass through a handful of chokepoints: auction markets, feedyards, packers and brand-inspected private sales. Watching the exits is cheaper and harder to game than counting the pasture. The barn has legal exposure and is a willing data supplier, whereas the borrower is not. Lender pledge data is a cornered resource: once enough lenders load it, no producer-side software vendor can replicate the registry without the lenders.
first_30_days: October is the peak calf run. Sign one mid-size sale barn (offering free service plus a sale-day lien report) and three nearby lenders who already send lien notices. Build manually, with a sheet and a fuzzy-match script. The barn emails the consignment list Monday or Tuesday, we match it against lender profiles (20-50 loans to start) and send text or email alerts within hours. Log every hit, the head at stake and whether the lender already knew, for four weeks. Aim for one or two consignments a lender did not know about, and turn them into an anonymized case. In week 4 ask each lender for $300/loan/yr on a minimum of 20 loans, and ask the barn for two more barns in its trade area. Confirm with counsel how Food Security Act lien-notice rules and state central-filing systems interact with the alerts.

competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: CattleMax, AgriWebb, IMI Global / Where Food Comes From (Beef Passport), Merck Animal Health (Allflex tags/readers, Vence). White space: Caveat first: the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was already spent when I started, so I ran zero searches. The biggest gap is that I could not identify the third-party collateral-inspection firms that lenders already pay for cattle counts, or any startup selling vet-verified herd inventory to lenders. Do not treat 'gap' as 'open'.

The vendors were CattleMax, AgriWebb, IMI Global/WFCF, Ceres Tag, Halter, HerdDogg and Gallagher. Merck/Vence returned 403, so I could not check it. IMI Global's Beef Passport ties EIDs to verification records for the supply chain, not to liens or exits. State central-filing systems and brand agencies are passive, annual or paper-based lists, so we sit on top of them and can partner.
