title: Unbundling Edits for Pet Insurance Claims
one_liner: Give pet insurers the claim-edit engine human health has had for 30 years: canonical procedure codes, bundling rules, and price benchmarks for messy vet invoices.
customer: Pet insurance MGAs, carriers and TPAs adjudicating roughly 100k to 2M claims a year, the mid-size players without in-house claims data science. Later, corporate veterinary groups and pet-owner pre-treatment estimate checks.
problem: Veterinary invoices are free-text line items exported from practice-management systems, with no universal procedure code set and no NCCI-style edits. Adjusters hand-review them. Insurers cannot tell that the vet billed anesthesia monitoring, an IV catheter, fluids and the e-collar as separate lines on top of a surgery fee, or what a routine dental cleaning costs in a given ZIP code. Claim severity is inflating with vet consolidation, and insurers answer with blanket premium hikes instead of line-level accuracy.
solution: An API that ingests invoice PDFs or line items. An LLM plus a hand-built taxonomy of the top ~300 vet procedures (about 80% of spend) normalizes each line to a canonical code. A rules layer, built the way NCCI and medically-unlikely edits work, flags unbundling, duplicates and implausible units. A benchmark layer returns usual-and-customary ranges by ZIP and practice type. The adjuster sees pay, reduce or review, with reason codes.
why_now: There are roughly 7 million insured US pets, and the segment is growing at double-digit rates with loss-ratio and price-hike pressure. Corporate vet consolidation is raising invoice complexity. LLMs make invoice line-item normalization, the hard part that took human-health edit vendors years, cheap enough for a two-person team.
revenue_model: Per-claim fee of $0.25-$0.75, or 10-15% of validated savings. A 500k-claim MGA is worth $150-350k a year. Add a benchmark-data license for vet chains and an owner-facing estimate checker later.
non_obvious_insight: Every automation wave in healthcare billing started with standardized codes and claim edits, not with AI. Cotiviti and Optum are basically edit libraries with sales teams. Pet insurance is at the pre-CPT stage. Someone who has spent years living inside code sets, bundling logic and 'this is included in the global fee' arguments can build the missing layer in weeks. Insurers will not fund a fight with vets. They will fund a neutral, consistent, explainable edit that does not vary by adjuster.
first_30_days: Recruit one ex-coder (CPC) and a vet tech consultant. Build the 300-line taxonomy from public estimate sheets and a few hundred sample invoices. Approach 10 pet-insurance MGAs and TPAs with a free retrospective: run 5,000 of their anonymized past invoices and report the dollar share found in bundled, duplicate or out-of-range lines. Convert the best result into a paid pilot on per-claim pricing.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: VetControl (Illingen, Germany), Five Sigma (Clive AI claims adjuster), Sirma (custom ML for PetsBest, now under Synchrony), FairVet. White space: Nobody I found sells a US, insurer-facing, explainable edit library (canonical line-item codes, bundling and duplicate rules, unit plausibility, reason codes) with cross-carrier benchmarks, to mid-size MGAs and TPAs.

- VetControl is the only true direct analog, and it is German, GOT-based, a services-plus-software hybrid, and shows no US customers.
- Five Sigma and Sirma classify line items for coverage, not for pricing or bundling.
- FairVet and Vet Receipt hold consumer-sourced benchmark data with no insurer-grade normalization.
- Trupanion and Lassie built in-house and are not customers.
- Verisk has standardized the policy side only.

The unserved gap is an invoice-derived, ZIP-level, procedure-level price index built from insurer claims, which no owner-upload app can match in volume. It would be joined to explainable pay/reduce/review decisions for mid-size carriers with no data science team.

Structural risk to flag. Human-health edits work because of provider contracts and CMS rules. Pet insurers have no contracts with vets and no 'global fee' concept, and they pay owners by reimbursement. Line-level reductions therefore land on policyholders as balance bills, which invites complaints and regulatory attention. I found no US insurer RFP or public spend for this. The demand evidence is indirect: cost inflation, plus vendors like VetControl selling a similar product in Germany.

title: Neutral Baselines and Neighbor Guarantees for Data Centers
one_liner: A neutral third party installs pre-construction sensors around proposed data centers and administers a developer-funded, automatic payout guarantee to neighbors, so permit fights run on evidence.
customer: Independent and mid-size data center developers seeking 50-500 MW campus approvals in contested counties. County commissions and state regulators are a second buyer because they can make the service a permit condition. Hyperscalers with in-house community teams are not the target.
problem: Permit fights are evidence-poor. Nobody has a pre-construction baseline of well levels, night-time noise, air quality or voltage at homes, so every later complaint about dry wells or a hum can be neither proven nor disproven. Both sides fight on feelings and lawyers. Politics has turned: New York paused environmental permits for data centers of 50 MW or more in July 2026, Texas ordered its environmental regulator to stop issuing new data center permits in September 2026, and local pauses now exist in at least 14 states. A Reuters/Ipsos poll found only 14% of Americans would welcome one nearby.
solution: Baseline-in-a-Box. Over 60-90 days before the application, deploy 30-60 low-cost sensors: property-line night noise, depth and conductivity in volunteer neighbors' wells, PM2.5, night-sky brightness, and voltage sag at homes. Publish a read-only public dashboard. Have a university extension hydrogeologist and an acoustician review the methods. Escrow the data with hash-anchored timestamps so neither side can edit it. Keep monitoring for 10 years. Then add a Neighbor Guarantee: a developer-funded escrow that pays affected households automatically, like parametric crop insurance, when verified well drawdown or noise exceedances occur. No lawsuit is needed.
why_now: In 2026 the moratorium movement jumped from town boards to governors' offices (New York's executive order of July 14, Texas's TCEQ permit halt of September 21). Developers now need social license as much as megawatts, and regulators are actively drafting the frameworks that will say what evidence counts.
revenue_model: The developer pays $75-150k per site for setup, $4-10k per month for monitoring, and an 8-10% administration fee on the guarantee escrow. Counties that write the service into permit conditions create repeat demand. Later, anonymized data licensing to regulators and insurers.
non_obvious_insight: The baseline protects the developer more than the opponents. It is the only defense against future exaggerated or mistaken claims, and it turns 'trust us' into 'audit us'. Parametric payouts replace adversarial claims, which is why a rational developer buys it from a neutral party rather than opposing it.
first_30_days: Pick one county with a pending rezoning hearing (Georgia, Virginia, Indiana, Pennsylvania or Texas). Offer the developer's land agent a free 30-day pilot on 10 neighbor wells with an agricultural-extension partner. Build nodes from off-the-shelf parts at about $1.5-3k each. Present the live dashboard at the public hearing and convert that developer to a paid contract. Use the result as the case study for the next 5 developers.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: KETOS (SHIELD / KELP data-center water monitoring), Aethair (Aethair PRO, Environet, Thiamis), Envirosuite (ASX:EVS), Kunak. White space: Nobody found sells the bundle, so the status is 'gap' and not 'open'. The sensor and baseline layer is not open: KETOS (about $45M raised) pitches an independent baseline for data centers, Aethair pitches pre-construction baselines, Envirosuite has community dashboards, and consultancies bundle baselines into permitting. The unserved wedge is what sits on top of the sensors. (1) A neutral administrator holding escrowed, tamper-evident data whose governance the county and community accept, unlike developer-hired consultants and unlike opposition-side groups such as CEDS. (2) The Neighbor Guarantee: an automatic, no-litigation payout to households from a developer-funded escrow when a pre-agreed trigger is hit. No vendor, insurer, county ordinance or developer program found does this. The nearest things are Franklin County, Indiana's draft rule (escrow for 24-hour emergency potable water to impacted neighbors, plus developer-funded monitoring wells), one-off buyouts and lump-sum checks. (3) A 10-year, multi-parameter (wells, noise, PM2.5, voltage) record packaged as a permit-condition template that regulators can adopt. Weak points: the sensor baseline will commoditize; attribution is hard, because well drawdown from drought or other pumping is indistinguishable from data-center drawdown unless the design uses upgradient control wells and pumping records; automatic payouts may look like insurance under state law; and developer counsel may resist a pre-committed payout as an admission of liability. Note: the web-search budget ran out before I could check Crunchbase/YC directly for a startup doing exactly the escrow-plus-parametric bundle, so 'nobody found' means no evidence in about 25 searches, not proof of absence.

title: Family Bank: Bank of Mom and Dad, Papered
one_liner: A family office's real job is governance and records, not investing; for $20/mo, give ordinary parents and adult children a promissory-note, autopay and sibling-fairness ledger for the money that already flows between them.
customer: Parents aged 55-75 who lend or give money to adult children (down-payment help, car, tuition, debt payoff, business start), sold as a pair with the adult child (28-45). Elder-law attorneys, mortgage brokers and credit unions are referral channels.
problem: Family lending is handshake-based. Zero-interest loans over $10k invite imputed-interest questions. Gifts above the $19,000 annual exclusion (2026) need Form 709 filings. Medicaid's 60-month look-back treats gifts and forgiven loans as transfers. Mortgage lenders want documented gift letters. Siblings fight at inheritance over who got what because nobody kept records. NAR's 2025 profile shows the median first-time buyer is 40 and 22% received a gift or loan from relatives or friends.
solution: A guided flow decides gift vs loan and generates a note at or above the AFR (August 2026: 4.10% short, 4.35% mid, 4.92% long). ACH autopay collects and pays, and both sides get annual interest statements. A December 'forgiveness engine' forgives up to the exclusion with proper letters. A sibling ledger records every advancement so estates can equalize. Flags fire for Form 709 and Medicaid look-back exposure, and there is a mortgage-ready gift-letter generator plus one-click export to the family's estate attorney. Attorney review is an add-on.
why_now: Median first-time buyer age hit 40 (a record), housing costs push more family help, and long-term-care costs make the Medicaid look-back a live worry for boomer parents. Instant-payment and bank-linking rails make autopay cheap. The 2026 federal estate exemption is $15M, so for most families the value is peace and records, not tax planning.
revenue_model: $20/mo per family (up to 3 active loans); $49 document packs for the free-to-paid funnel; $149 attorney review add-on with referral fees; optional servicing fee; later, a pooled family reserve product.
non_obvious_insight: The killer feature is not the loan, it is the sibling ledger. Most family money fights are about unequal treatment nobody can prove, and family offices solve this with an advancement ledger that ordinary families never get. The loan-vs-gift label is also the pivot point for tax and Medicaid consequences, so classification is the paid moment.
first_30_days: Ship a free AFR calculator and note generator aimed at 'family loan agreement' searches, and sell $49 document packs. Convert 5% to the $20/mo servicing tier. Line up 3 elder-law attorneys who receive leads and review notes. Target 50 paying families.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: LoanBack, FamZoo, Wealth.com, Vanilla. White space: Research was limited: the WebSearch budget was exhausted (200 of 200) before any planned search ran, so I worked only from direct fetches of specific pages. I did not search Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, forums or RFPs, and I could not check LegalZoom, Rocket Lawyer or Nolo because those URLs returned 404 or 403. What the evidence shows: (1) The document layer is already commoditized. LoanBack sells a note plus amortization schedule for $15 to $30 and has 10+ years of traction, so the free AFR calculator and $49 note pack in the 30-day plan would compete head-on with it. (2) Nothing I found does the parts that are the real product. I checked LoanBack, FamZoo, Wealth.com and Vanilla, and none advertises these: real ACH autopay between parent and adult child; annual interest statements for both parties; a December forgiveness engine that applies the annual gift exclusion; a gift-vs-loan classification flow tied to Form 709 and Medicaid look-back flags; a mortgage gift-letter generator; a sibling advancement ledger that estates can equalize from; a one-click export to the family's estate attorney. (3) The sibling ledger and the classification audit trail appear genuinely unserved for ordinary families. The advisor-only estate tools (Wealth.com, Vanilla) do not sell to a 62-year-old parent or her adult child. (4) Coverage gap: I could not confirm the absence of niche competitors. Private-note servicers, small startups and attorney-firm tools may exist that my fetches missed.

title: Smoke Report Autopsy for Policyholder Advocates
one_liner: An adequacy auditor that scores any carrier-side smoke, ash and soot report against a public, versioned sampling grid. It then drafts the AB 1795 deficiency letter and supplemental sampling plan, and sells to public adjusters and plaintiff attorneys in the Eaton and Palisades zones.
customer: Wedge: 15-25 licensed public adjuster firms working standing-home smoke claims in Altadena, Pasadena, Pacific Palisades and Malibu, plus 3-5 plaintiff firms running the Ghazarian-style class actions against carrier-retained hygiene vendors. Later: homeowners buying direct at about $295, then carrier claims-legal teams running pre-flight audits on their own vendors.
problem: Every standing-home claimant holds a carrier-vendor IH report saying 'clean' or 'minor'. Neither the public adjuster nor the attorney can tell quickly whether it was under-sampled. Carrier-retained hygienists reportedly take about 10 samples in 3,000 sq ft, skip attics, wall cavities and HVAC, and compare results to urban background dust. A CIH second opinion costs $2k-$4k+ and takes weeks from a scarce pool. Purdue's free review is capacity-limited and does not produce claim-ready output. From Jan 1, 2027 AB 1795 makes insurers pay for testing that is 'necessary', but only if someone shows what is necessary and missing.
solution: Upload the IH report and lab PDF. LLM extraction with human QA pulls sample count, locations, media (wipe, tape lift, air, bulk), comparison basis, detection limits and skipped zones. It scores them against a public 'Adequacy Grid' built from AIHA's wildfire guide, IICRC/RIA/CIRI, 40 CFR 745.227 and 8 CCR 1529, with every criterion cited. Within 48 hours the customer gets a 2-page scorecard listing what was not sampled, a statute-cited deficiency letter for the PA or attorney to send, and a supplemental sampling plan that a partner CIH-of-record can sign, with a priced quote from a partner testing firm. The plaintiff tier ingests hundreds of reports in batch for pattern analytics (share with zero attic samples, samples per 1,000 sq ft by vendor). The grid is versioned so it re-maps when DTSC publishes standards in 2028-29. We do not sample, employ technicians, or give expert opinions.
why_now: AB 1795 was signed 9/15/2026 and takes effect 1/1/2027. It creates a 30-day inspection duty and a duty to pay for necessary testing, and it presumes smoke, ash and soot in a standing home came from the fire. Class actions over vendor sampling were filed in Feb 2026, LA County sued State Farm on 8/31/2026, and 13,000+ standing homes with smoke damage are in play. Cheap LLM document extraction makes a 48-hour, hundreds-of-dollars audit feasible where it used to be a $3k CIH engagement.
revenue_model: Public adjusters pay $395 per audit, or $2,500 a month for up to 10 active files. The CIH-signed supplemental sampling plan costs $900, split 50/50 with the partner CIH. Plaintiff-firm pattern analytics run $40k-$150k per engagement, for example a 300-report batch. The partner testing firm pays a flat referral fee on supplemental sampling it wins, or we take none if that raises fee-splitting concerns. Phase 2 sells carrier claims-legal teams a $2k-$5k per-vendor-report pre-flight audit. Bottom-up: even 15% of 13,000 homes at $395 plus a few analytics contracts is about $1.5M-$2.5M in year one, so the wedge is small and the dataset is the asset.
non_obvious_insight: The unit of leverage is the omission list, not the test result. AB 1795 obliges the insurer to pay for necessary testing, and a scored list of what was not sampled and why it matters converts a fuzzy fight into a checklist the adjuster must answer in writing. Every audit also writes one structured row (vendor, square footage, samples, comparator, zones skipped), so the tool quietly builds the largest labeled dataset of how carrier vendors sample. Counter-positioning is real: HygieneTech, Rimkus and Safeguard cannot sell a tool that indicts carrier-side sampling without alienating their own clients.
first_30_days: Week 1: collect 25 real IH reports with consent from EFRU volunteers, two public adjusters and one attorney. Sign two CIHs at about $150/hr to review the rubric, and a toxicologist as advisor. Weeks 2-3: build Grid v0.1 as a spreadsheet plus extraction pipeline, targeting over 90% field-level accuracy on the 25 reports. Run free 48-hour audits for 10 PA files. Track whether the deficiency letter gets the carrier or FAIR Plan to authorize additional testing. Week 4: start charging $395 from audit #11, aiming for 30 paid audits and one attorney LOI for a 100-report batch pilot at about $25k. Before day 15, confirm from the chaptered AB 1795 text that there is no qualified-person or licensure rule that blocks a non-CIH from drafting a sampling plan for CIH signature.
lineage: mutation of I0715 ('Interim Smoke-Damage Protocol Before the State Standard'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Hygiene Technologies International (HygieneTech), Rimkus, Safeguard EnviroGroup (Brad Kovar), EHS Analytical Solutions. White space: Mostly assessment supply and free guidance are crowded, so the raw 'do smoke testing' and 'publish a protocol' layers are not white space. Dozens of CIH-led firms sell $2k-$4k+ assessments and clearance certificates. AIHA, IICRC/RIA/CIRI, Purdue and EFRU already publish free or cheap protocols. Safeguard EnviroGroup is already pitching a 'defensible framework' to carriers. State agencies (AB 1795 drafts) planned to certify IHs, contractors and labs, which undercuts the training-fee line.

Still unserved: (1) Carrier and TPA operations under AB 1795. Nobody offers a claim-level compliance layer with the 30-day inspection clock, an audit-ready sampling plan mapped to zones, chain-of-custody records and an evidence file, sold as software. Carriers are 'technically opposed' but must comply from 1/1/2027, and CAT surge capacity is the pain. (2) Sampling-design defensibility. The fight is over how many samples, where, and against what background, and no independent tool scores a sampling plan or existing IH report for adequacy, though this is what class actions and the Purdue review turn on. (3) A neutral, versioned crosswalk from AIHA/IICRC/40 CFR 745.227 lead-dust levels and 8 CCR 1529 asbestos to a per-home plan, which updates when DTSC issues standards in 2028-29. (4) Pooled, structured sampling data across claims, which is what regulators reuse. EFRU holds only a few dozen homes.

Two facts weaken the 'vacuum' framing. Interim lead and asbestos thresholds already exist in AB 1642 (40 CFR 745.227(e)(8)(viii) and 8 CCR 1529). The vacuum is mainly sampling design and non-lead contaminants such as cyanide, other metals and dioxins.

Structural risks: the buyer conflict, because carriers may not adopt a protocol seen as policyholder-friendly and policyholder-side buyers want a testifying CIH rather than software. Remote IH sign-off and technician-collected samples may run into CIH and certification expectations. Any advantage is capped at the moment DTSC publishes standards.

Research limits: my web-search budget ran out before I could run Crunchbase, YC and TechCrunch-specific queries. The general startup searches (wildfire smoke assessment startup, chain-of-custody kits, technician network) found only wildfire-detection companies (Pano AI, FireScan, FireSafe AI), none in post-fire smoke-damage assessment. Treat 'no funded startup' as probable, not proven. | How this version avoids them: HygieneTech, Rimkus, Safeguard EnviroGroup, EHS Analytical, Home BioTesting and Vert-type shops all sell sampling supply and are either carrier-conflicted or capacity-bound. We sell no sampling, so EHS and Home BioTesting become the partners who fulfil the supplemental plans and gain lead flow. Purdue's free review is bounded by grad-student capacity and has no claim-language deliverable, SLA or batch mode; we cite its method and offer a data-share and donation instead of competing. IICRC, AIHA and EFRU publish guidance and maps but sell no per-claim operational tool, so we build on them and ask EFRU for a data partnership. Safeguard's 'defensible framework' is a carrier-side essay, whereas ours is a scoring engine aimed at the policyholder side. State standards in 2028-29 change the grid's contents but not the need for an audit tool, so the business survives the standard rather than dying with it.

title: Daubert-Ready Sample Audits for Litigation Surveys
one_liner: A neutral data-quality auditor that gives survey experts and litigators a signed, control-calibrated audit of the respondent sample behind a Lanham Act, false-advertising or damages survey, or a teardown of the other side's sample.
customer: Wedge: the 30-60 US testifying survey experts and boutique survey-litigation consultancies who field likelihood-of-confusion, secondary-meaning, deception and conjoint-damages surveys, plus the IP and false-advertising litigation partners who retain them. Later: in-house counsel at CPG and pharma companies that run claim-substantiation surveys for FTC or NAD challenges.
problem: A litigation survey is only worth what survives cross-examination and a Rule 702 challenge. Until recently 'we removed speeders and failed attention checks' was an adequate answer on sample quality. Agents now pass those checks (99.8% of 6,000 trials in the parent's evidence), so the standard defence is hollow. Opposing experts can attack the panel, and the amended Rule 702 (Dec 2023) makes the proponent show reliability by a preponderance. Survey experts have no neutral way to show their sample is clean, and rebuttal experts have no fast, credible way to quantify contamination in the other side's produced respondent data. The fee is small next to the $50k-$300k+ a litigation survey costs (from background knowledge, to be verified in calls) and the case value behind it.
solution: Two case-driven products. (1) Proponent audit: before full fielding, insert canary and honeypot items (with the expert's sign-off) and run a pilot. Ingest detection signals licensed from dtect, Verisoul or DQC rather than building an ensemble. Field the test and control cells on a 150-300-complete slice of a licensed address-recruited panel (NORC, Ipsos or Verasight-style, resold, not built). Deliver contamination-adjusted net-effect estimates with bounds, a sensitivity table ('conclusion holds up to X% contamination') and a hash-timestamped chain-of-custody field log. A named academic methodologist signs a declaration that can be attached to the expert report. (2) Rebuttal teardown: a fixed-scope 10-business-day analysis of the opposing side's produced respondent-level data, built to fit rebuttal-report deadlines. The firm never opines on the merits (confusion, deception, damages). It only certifies or attacks data quality, so it is a supplier to every expert rather than a competitor.
why_now: Agents that pass attention checks (2025-26) killed the old defence. Pew's Aug 2026 finding of 18% bogus respondents in opt-in samples, with trap questions and Sentry disagreeing on who is bogus, gives opposing counsel a citable, public source. The Dec 2023 Rule 702 amendment gives judges an explicit mandate to scrutinise reliability. The first contested Daubert motion where an expert cannot rebut agent contamination will spread fast through the small survey-expert community.
revenue_model: $12-40k per case engagement (proponent audit or rebuttal teardown), billed to the law firm as consulting-expert cost and passed through to the client. $60-120k/yr retainers for survey-expert firms that run 8-15 surveys a year, covering unlimited pilots and field-log stamps. $2-5k per survey for a hash-stamped field log as a low-touch add-on. Later, a $25-50k/yr library subscription for in-house claim-substantiation teams. Gross margin is mostly the licensed control slice (about $3-8k per engagement) plus methodologist hours.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is not paying for truth. The buyer is paying, with the client's litigation budget, for insurance against cross-examination, so willingness to pay is set by case value and not by the $/complete price that caps every other idea in this space. The test-versus-control design used in litigation surveys also means random-answering bots hit both cells and pull net confusion toward zero. Contamination therefore tends to hurt plaintiffs and help defendants, so both sides have a reason to buy: proponents to insulate, opponents to attack. Once a court admits or credits the method, it becomes citable precedent. That is process power and switching cost that no detection API can copy.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: list every survey expert named in published Lanham Act opinions of the last five years and 40 IP litigation partners. Run 10 price-validation calls (5 experts, 5 partners) and stop if fewer than 4 say $15k+ is reasonable. Days 10-25: buy about 300 completes each from 4 panel vendors on a classic Eveready-format and Teflon-format design, plus a 150-complete control slice from a licensed address-recruited panel. Measure how many bots it takes to swing net confusion by 5 points. Days 20-30: publish 'How many agents does it take to flip a confusion survey?' as a white paper and CLE talk proposal. Offer two free rebuttal teardowns on public-record survey data in exchange for permission to cite. Sign one academic survey methodologist as chief methodologist and testifier.
lineage: mutation of I0716 ('Independent Referee for Survey Panel Data'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Data Quality Co-op (DQC), Verasight, Verisoul, CloudResearch (Sentry, Engage, Bot Olympics). White space: Detection is crowded and getting cheap: Verisoul, Roundtable, dtect, CloudResearch, Kantar Qubed, Research Defender, PureScore, ReDem and CleanID all sell it, some at cents per respondent. Cross-supplier scorecards already exist too, since Data Quality Co-op is a neutral clearinghouse. Building a detection ensemble or a generic vendor scorecard would be a fifth-to-tenth entrant against funded players.

What I did not find anyone selling:
1. A per-study ground-truth calibration. This means running a slice of the same questionnaire on a verified, address-recruited human control group and then reporting contamination-adjusted estimates with error bounds. Every vendor I found detects and removes. None quantifies how much bias survives the cleaning, and none re-estimates the result against a known-real reference. Pew's finding that voter-file matching removed valid respondents and made the error worse suggests 'remove the flagged' is itself a source of bias.
2. A neutral buyer-side referee that owns no sample. dtect is neutral but only sells entry-time detection. DQC is neutral but does not audit individual studies or supply a control sample. Verasight owns verified humans but sells sample.
3. Independent, third-party verification of the vendors' own accuracy claims. CloudResearch and Verisoul each claim 100% agent detection from internal or self-run tests. The Bot Olympics is MIT-judged but tests CloudResearch's own system.

The missing piece for a startup is the control panel. Building an address-recruited, device-attested panel of about 2,000 people is slow and expensive. The likelier route is to partner with or license an existing one (Verasight, NORC, Pew or Ipsos-style panels), not recruit from scratch.

This conclusion has limits. My WebSearch budget ran out at 200 calls, so I could not run the Crunchbase, YC or Product Hunt checks or search for a second wave of small startups. I also could not confirm funding for DQC, Roundtable, dtect or Verasight. | How this version avoids them: Detection vendors (Verisoul, dtect, Roundtable, CloudResearch, ReDem, CleanID) sell entry-time filtering to panels at cents per complete and produce nothing a court can use. They are input suppliers here. Data Quality Co-op's scorecard and Data Trust Score describe suppliers in general and do not give a case-specific, testifiable declaration. Verasight owns verified humans but sells sample, so opposing counsel would call it conflicted. Pew and NORC publish the methodology for free but not per case, and not in expert-report form. Panel-owner stacks (Kantar Qubed, Research Defender, PureScore, Pori) are the self-grading problem that Daubert challenges target. Existing litigation-survey consultancies field surveys and testify on merits, so they are customers, not rivals.

title: Fees-in-Kind: Harvest Becomes School Fee Credit
one_liner: A weigh-in and ledger service that lets parents pay school fees with maize, beans and potatoes at a transparent price, while schools get cheaper, steadier food supply.
customer: Boards of management, principals and bursars of public boarding and day secondary schools, including the new senior-school cohorts, plus rural private schools. The end users are smallholder parents in maize, bean and potato zones.
problem: Farm households are asset-rich and cash-poor exactly when fees fall due in January, May and August. Schools already accept 'a tin of maize' informally, but the value is whatever the storekeeper or bursar decides, with no receipts. Meanwhile the same schools buy food through brokers at inflated tender prices, and government capitation often arrives late. Children still get sent home over arrears even when the parents' store is full of grain. Food is often the largest line in a boarding school's budget.
solution: A Fee Credit Ledger. Farmers deliver graded produce to the school store or a village collection point. A standard weigh ticket (photo of the scale plus a moisture reading) generates an SMS receipt, and the value is credited to the learner's fee account at a published reference price such as NCPB or the county market average, minus a small handling margin. The school gets a weekly reconciliation. On the buying side, the platform, registered as an AGPO-eligible youth or women group (check how each school's procurement committee applies the 30% reservation), bids for school food supply and sources from the same parents. It pools, grades and quality-checks (moisture, aflatoxin spot test). An add-on is hermetic storage bags on credit so parents can deliver later in the term rather than dumping at harvest.
why_now: The first CBC cohort entered senior school in January 2026, expanding boarding and food demand, and the next cohort arrives in January 2027, so schools are planning Term 1 supply now. Capitation delays keep squeezing school food budgets. Cheap Bluetooth scales, moisture meters and M-Pesa and SMS receipts make a trustworthy weigh ticket trivial. Principals in Kenya talk in tight associations, so one working pilot spreads fast.
revenue_model: A 4-8% handling margin on food flow: schools pay below their current broker-inclusive price and farmers receive above the broker price. Later a per-learner per-term ledger fee (about KES 50-100). Once the ledger produces credit-quality data, short-term financing of fee arrears or school receivables.
non_obvious_insight: In every rural ward the school is the largest, most predictable institutional food buyer, and the 'fee arrears list' is a timing and valuation mismatch, not poverty. Fintechs treat barter as embarrassing or informal, but for smallholders paying in maize is the default. What is missing is fair valuation and a ledger everyone trusts. The AGPO set-aside is an under-used entry ticket for farmer groups into school tenders.
first_30_days: Sign 2-3 principals through your own old high school or a heads' association branch meeting for a one-term pilot in January 2027. Buy two Bluetooth hanging scales and moisture meters (a few hundred dollars), run the ledger on Google Sheets plus Africa's Talking SMS, and recruit 100 parent households at PTA meetings. Set the price at the midpoint between the farmgate broker price and the school tender price. Register the entity for AGPO and open a supplier profile with the school.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Maziwa ni School Fees (Uasin Gishu County + Space AI + Tuiyo Farmers Cooperative), Food4Education (Tap2Eat), Zeraki (Zeraki Finance), SchoolPay (Uganda, Kenya, Zambia). White space: Nobody I found offers a grain, bean or potato fee-credit ledger for schools. Google News, site fetches and GitHub search turned up no startup, cooperative product or open-source tool that gives standard weigh tickets, SMS receipts and a published reference price. The practice is real but informal, and it is ripe for a trust layer.

Unserved specifics:
(1) Secondary boarding and senior schools in maize, bean and potato zones. Uasin Gishu has taken dairy, and Food4Education owns primary school meals.
(2) Fair valuation and receipts for staples. Principal Kegoro at Nyabisia Secondary (Kisii) says 'we accept them to bring maize or beans, then we value them and receipt them', which is exactly the informal, discretionary step to standardise.
(3) A per-school reconciliation of in-kind credit against arrears lists. Zeraki Finance and SchoolPay show no in-kind receipt type.
(4) Linking fee credit to the school's own kitchen demand, so the grain never needs to be sold on.

Risks that shrink the white space:
(a) The supply-side tender and AGPO piece is weak. IDRC reports only 1-2% of AGPO opportunities reach women, youth and disability-owned firms, with 90-day-plus payment delays and kickback demands. Schools buy 65% from brokers by manual tender.
(b) 2026 is a maize shortage year. The deficit is about 5.4M bags, flour is at KES 153-163 per 2kg, and 53% of smallholders cite lack of surplus. Farmers may hold grain back, and valuation disputes will be sharp.
(c) Tickets for day schools are small. The proposed day-school fee is KES 7,675, against KES 53k-88k for boarding.
(d) One entity being fee-credit collector and tender supplier to the same school invites a conflict-of-interest problem.
(e) Storekeepers and brokers benefit from the current opacity.
(f) Absence from news is not proof of absence. WebSearch was exhausted and Crunchbase and Product Hunt were blocked, so a stealth or very small pilot cannot be ruled out.

title: Keep-Warm: Preserving Power in Idle Plants
one_liner: Invert the database: instead of scoring dead plants once, sell a monthly service that keeps their electrical service alive and monitored, then turn 200 preserved shells into a right-of-first-offer inventory and, later, a balance-sheet powered-shell bank.
customer: Wedge: banks, special servicers and lenders holding real-estate-owned industrial plants, plus corporate owners of mothballed plants and county land banks, in the Mahoning Valley and Akron/Canton first. Later buyers: data-center, battery and manufacturing developers who pay for shells certified 'energized-ready'.
problem: An idle plant's electrical system is a wasting asset on a clock. Standard commercial property policies limit cover for vandalism, theft, water damage and sprinkler leakage once a building has been vacant for about 60 days (an assumption to verify with an insurance broker), copper theft and roof leaks wreck switchgear, utilities can pull service or reclassify accounts on idle meters, oil-filled transformers degrade, and permit fees and reports lapse. Residential-style property-preservation firms winterize and change locks, but nobody is paid to preserve amps. Owners find out the plant is worth far less than it was only when a buyer's electrician opens the gear two years later.
solution: Two tiers. 'Watch' at $650 per month: baseline electrician record (the Power Passport becomes the set-up fee), a $600 sensor kit (humidity, temperature, door, current clamps on the main service, cellular camera), quarterly thermography, and an insurer-facing monthly report. 'Warm' at $2,200 per month: monthly electrician visits, keep-energized management with the utility including minimum-bill and account status, annual transformer oil sampling, dehumidification, theft-alarm response and permit fee and report compliance. The continuous data produces an 'energized-ready' score, days to first power, and a verified time series no one-off inspection can match. Marketing and right-of-first-offer rights are bundled into the contract for owners who want a sale.
why_now: Low-cost cellular sensors and cameras collapsed to tens of dollars a unit. Vision models now read nameplates and gear photos cheaply, which cuts analyst hours per building. More industrial shells are going idle while buyers now pay a premium for existing power, so, for the first time, preserving the electrical system has a positive return.
revenue_model: Recurring: $650 or $2,200 per building per month plus a $2,500 baseline record; a carry-cost comparison shows a 300k sq ft idle plant costing an owner roughly $15k-$40k per month, so the service is 3-8% on top of existing carry. Gross margin about 50-55% at 10 buildings per electrician route. Insurer angle: partner with a vacant-property insurance managing general agent to turn monitoring into a rating credit, which can pay for itself. Scale path: 200 buildings on Warm and Watch is about $4M-$5M annual recurring revenue; the contract's right of first offer gives inventory to sell to buyers on a fee basis; a later fund of $50M-$100M exercises options on the best 20 shells, subdivides them into permitted 'factory condos' or powered shells and sells or leases at a premium. First 6 months: 5-8 paying buildings.
non_obvious_insight: The same service that stops the asset dying also builds the only dataset that matters: a time series of load, temperature, humidity and access on hundreds of idle industrial buildings, and exclusive access to a pipeline of them. That combination is a cornered resource plus a switching cost, defended by contracts and data history and not by scoring algorithms anyone can copy. The parent is a snapshot; this is the movie, and a monthly bill is a better business than a report.
first_30_days: Week 1: list 40 idle plants owned by banks, special servicers and land banks from county auditor and REO data in two metros; contact 8 REO and asset managers. Week 2: call two vacant-property insurance brokers and one managing general agent to test whether monitoring earns a premium credit or a vacancy-clause endorsement (the riskiest assumption). Weeks 3-4: sign three 90-day pilots on Watch at a waived set-up fee in exchange for a case study and marketing rights, install kits, and deliver the first insurer-facing report. Success test: one lender converts to $650 per month paid and one insurer or broker confirms a written premium credit or vacancy accommodation.
lineage: mutation of I0820 ('Power Passport: Scoring Dead Factories on Amps, Permits'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Brownfield.ai, Scout (ScoutCities), LandGate, Enverus Site & Screen. White space: Nobody I found productises a building-level, physically verified 'inside-the-fence' record for dead Midwest plants. That record would cover the electrician-verified main service size, voltage, gear age and nameplates, spare capacity, slab and crane-rail condition, the state of the existing air and wastewater permits, and a utility will-serve letter, all in a scored, comparable format sold before the deal. The funded players (LandGate, Enverus, GridCARE, Paces) work at the substation and grid level and are aimed at data centers. Utility and state databases (JobsOhio, AEP, FirstEnergy, ZoomProspector) verify sites and utility service, not building gear or permit status. Scout and Brownfield.ai are the closest competitors, but they look desktop- and network-led with no per-building inspection, and I found no evidence they carry electrician-verified data. The genuine gap is a trusted, standardised, seller-commissioned building electrical and permit record, not the parcel-scoring layer, which is already crowded and funded. The idea's weaker points: the Ohio permit-transferability wedge is thin (see evidence), and it is unproven that brokers will pay $1.5k-$3.5k. | How this version avoids them: None of the parent's competitors monitor or preserve anything. Brownfield.ai, Scout, LandGate, Enverus, GridCARE, Paces and ZoomProspector sell data or listings, and JobsOhio and the utility databases are free lists. PCA and electrical inspection firms sell a one-time report, and residential property-preservation and big facilities-management firms cover occupied, high-value assets or locks and lawns, not energized-capacity preservation. The business is recurring service revenue with a proprietary time series, so a funded data competitor would have to hire electricians and sign owner contracts to copy it, and the exclusive marketing rights become a cornered resource.

title: Delay-Suit Rails for Stuck Immigration Cases
one_liner: White-label filing infrastructure that lets solo immigration lawyers file mandamus/APA delay lawsuits in 48 hours, turning the government's habit of mooting suits into a flat-fee product.
customer: Solo and small immigration firms (1-10 attorneys) who pay a per-filing platform fee; end clients (naturalization, green card and employment petition applicants) pay the firm a flat $2.5-5k. Secondary buyer: employers with stuck petitions.
problem: Cases are stuck well past posted processing times: interviewed N-400s never scheduled for oath, I-485s and I-140s idling, and holds or pauses applied to nationals of dozens of countries since late 2025. Clients wait 12-30 months. Lawyers know a federal delay suit often shakes a case loose, but most solos have never filed one. Drafting the complaint, civil cover sheet, summons, service on the U.S. Attorney's civil process clerk, the Attorney General and the agency, and district-specific local rules is a 6-10 hour learning curve, and no one wants to be the first to file.
solution: A web tool with three parts. (1) An eligibility screen: enter the receipt date, form type and field office, and it compares them to posted times and to real observed outcomes, then scores the delay claim. (2) A complaint and exhibit generator with a per-district rules library, a service-of-process checklist and deadline calendar (the 60-day government answer window), and a template for the joint status report or stipulated dismissal that follows adjudication. (3) A docket-outcome database that logs, by district, judge and case type, how long from filing to adjudication. The attorney of record signs every filing. The platform is software, not a law firm.
why_now: Through late 2025 and 2026 USCIS added enhanced vetting, holds and pauses on benefit requests tied to nationality, expanded re-review of approved cases, and slower naturalization and green card scheduling. The volume of genuinely stuck cases is at a decade high. Federal courts are also less deferential to agencies since the Loper Bright decision, and adjudicating a stuck case is cheaper for the government than defending it. Solos are overloaded and short of billable-hour alternatives, so a ready-made product for a high-ticket service is easy to sell.
revenue_model: $350-600 per filing charged to the law firm (flat, not a percentage, to avoid fee-splitting rules), or $299/month for up to 3 filings. Later: a paid intelligence tier of docket-outcome analytics by district, and a litigation-funding partnership for clients who can't front the fee.
non_obvious_insight: The lawsuit is rarely litigated to judgment. The U.S. Attorney's Office usually tells USCIS to adjudicate within 30-90 days so the suit can be dismissed as moot, so the client's real purchase is a forced deadline. Clients almost never hear about this because form-prep firms earn on the application, not on pressure. Posted processing times are also misleading (they reflect only completed cases at a percentile), so whoever accumulates real time-to-decision data by field office and district owns the moat.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 immigration attorneys in high-volume districts (N.D. Cal., S.D. Tex., D.N.J., E.D.N.Y., S.D. Fla.) and offer free templates for the first filing. Build the intake screen and three complaint templates first (delayed N-400 after interview, delayed I-485, delayed I-130/I-140 or a nationality hold). Concierge-run 10 filings by hand, charging the firms $400 each. Log every outcome date, since that dataset is the product. Post outcome stats to immigration-lawyer Facebook groups and AILA chapter listservs to pull in the next 30 firms.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Bertollini / Mandamus.com (immigration mandamus boutique), Docketwise (immigration case-management software), Alma (tryalma.com, immigration law firm plus tech), Boundless (consumer immigration services). White space: Important caveat first. The WebSearch budget was already spent (200 of 200) before I started, so I ran no web searches at all. I used direct fetches of guessed or known URLs, CourtListener's API and GitHub search. This means 'no direct software competitor found' is weaker evidence than normal. One attempt to load a Google results page returned nothing and was not used. Before committing, someone should run 6-8 real searches (for example 'mandamus AI immigration', 'delay lawsuit software immigration attorneys', Crunchbase, YC, and the AILA and AIC toolkits).

What I found: no software or platform that sells attorney-signed, white-label mandamus filing plus a per-district rules library plus outcome analytics to solo immigration lawyers. The only direct-service players are boutique law firms selling the suit to end clients. Mandamus.com does this at $5,000 plus $500 and gives away templates, and the practice-management incumbent Docketwise has no such feature. The open data (CourtListener) and free guides make the raw ingredients cheap for anyone.

The genuinely unserved wedge is narrow. It is a pre-filing 'will this get mooted or dismissed here' triage, based on real district-by-form-type outcome data, plus a ready-to-file pack for routine delays in the districts where the government usually adjudicates rather than litigates (per Mandamus.com's own data: EDNY, D. Conn., DNJ and EDMI at 83-85% voluntary dismissal after agency action).

Parts of the pitch look weak against what I found:
(1) Nationality-hold suits look poor. Per Mandamus.com's summary of 13 D.D.C. delay decisions from June to August 2026, the government won all 13. Judge Leon in the consolidated Ivanov case found the categorical pause unexplained but dismissed the delay and mandamus counts under TRAC and limited relief to named plaintiffs. A 'nationality hold' template is a liability, not a hook.
(2) S.D. Tex., one of the five launch districts, is hostile. Cheejati v. Blinken (5th Cir. 2024) bars I-485 delay claims on jurisdictional grounds, and DOJ there files motions to dismiss rather than negotiate.
(3) Buckhannon: when USCIS simply adjudicates, the plaintiff is not a prevailing party and can't recover EAJA fees (typically $4,000-$12,000 only if a consent order is obtained). The flat fee holds up, but the 'forced deadline' product should be structured around consent orders.
(4) The '6-10 hour learning curve' is being eroded by free content and general AI drafting.
(5) The data moat is thin. CourtListener docket data is free, and the boutique firms already publish their own district stats.

title: Real-Factory Credentials From Customs Shipping Records
one_liner: Turn public US import records into supplier-owned reputation credentials and audit-ready reasonable-care dossiers that prove a factory is a real manufacturer.
customer: Small and mid-size US importers of record (Amazon and Shopify brands, furniture, hardware and apparel distributors) re-sourcing to Vietnam, India, Mexico and Turkey. Customs brokers are a channel, and factories are the second payer.
problem: The importer of record is investigated first, and liability turns on whether it exercised reasonable care about the supplier's origin claims. In August 2026 the White House published a report on transshipment, a 40% penalty tariff applies, and CBP has expanded inspections of shipments from Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Mexico. Small importers cannot tell a real factory from a trading company or a re-labeller, and sourcing agents' claims are unverifiable.
solution: Supplier Proof. Build a profile per factory from three or more years of US import records (shipper and consignee names, volumes, product codes, ports, cadence) plus corporate registry and location data, flag anomalies such as volume beyond plausible capacity, mismatched product codes or shell-company addresses, and add optional local inspector visits. Factories claim and verify their profile and can consent to name repeat buyers as references. The output is a dossier the importer can hand to a broker or to CBP.
why_now: Tariff enforcement moved in 2025-26 from headline rates to origin verification, and the August 2026 transshipment report has put importer liability on every compliance officer's desk. Sourcing shifts away from China are happening now, so millions of dollars of orders are going to unfamiliar factories.
revenue_model: Importer subscriptions of $149-499 per month, $150-400 per dossier, inspector visits passed through at a margin, and $600-1,200 per year from factories for a verified credential once importers demand it.
non_obvious_insight: Import records are the only unforgeable cross-border reputation ledger for factories, but they are sold as raw rows to analysts. Repackaged as supplier-owned credentials with a reasonable-care wrapper, a data product becomes a compliance product with a real budget line: avoiding a 40% penalty.
first_30_days: Buy 12 months of import records for two categories (for example furniture and hardware from Vietnam and India). Auto-build about 1,000 factory profiles and hand-audit 20. Send 200 emails to sourcing managers and customs brokers. Sell the first 10 dossiers at $250 each and use them to refine the scoring.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ImportGenius, Panjiva (S&P Global Market Intelligence), Descartes Datamyne, ImportYeti. White space: The narrow wedge that appears unserved is a fixed-price, human-reviewed 'reasonable-care file' for a small US importer, sold through customs brokers. The SMB importer (Amazon or Shopify brand, or a $2-50M distributor) needs one factory checked before one PO. Enterprise tools (Sayari, Altana, Tradeverifyd, Trademo, Exiger) are sold by demo and are priced and scoped for large compliance teams. Data tools (ImportGenius, Panjiva, Datamyne, ImportYeti) sell rows and leave interpretation to the analyst. Inspectors (QIMA) and sourcing agents (Sourcify) sell physical checks, not a documentary file that maps to CBP's reasonable-care standard. The part I found nobody offering is a factory-claimed profile with consent-based buyer references, which is a two-sided credential. No visible player runs a supplier-owned reputation credential built on customs ledgers. However, the wedge is thin. (1) ImportGenius already markets 'supplier verification via shipping history' at the same $229-449/mo price band. (2) The raw-data floor is free or near-free. (3) Any one of Altana, Trademo or ImportGenius could add a 'transshipment risk report' feature quickly. (4) The factory-pays credential side has no demonstrated demand and needs a two-sided marketplace. Risks I could not check with the exhausted search budget: whether resale of licensed bill-of-lading data is allowed, that US import records often name the forwarder or trading company as shipper instead of the factory, that importers can request confidentiality under 19 CFR 103.31, and that no CBP safe-harbor exists for third-party dossiers.

title: Solar Job Escrow: Bankruptcy-Proof Project Records
one_liner: A neutral escrow that captures every financed solar job's permit, design, serial and step-in authorizations before the installer fails. The installer pays per job, the lender enforces deposits through milestone funding, and cure is paid from the final milestone the lender is still holding.
customer: Payer: mid-size residential installers (300-3,000 loan-financed jobs a year) that need financing access and a trust signal after Freedom Forever. Gatekeeper and co-seller: dealer-risk and credit heads at solar lenders and credit unions (GoodLeap, EverBright, EnFin, Credit Human-type), who can make escrow a dealer-tier condition. Channel: installer CRM, design and project-management platforms that embed the deposit.
problem: When an installer dies, the permits, interconnection applications, PE-stamped designs, serials and portal logins are locked in the dead company's name, and the lender starts from zero. Every other party (lender, homeowner, trustee) finds out after the fact. Before failure, all of that data exists and is easy to copy. After failure it is expensive to reconstruct. The parent product only starts once the loss has occurred, which is why it is lumpy, price-pressured and crowded.
solution: Each job auto-deposits a continuity pack at each milestone: signed contract, permit application and approval, PE-stamped design set, interconnection application number, equipment serials by BOM, and time-stamped site photos. Two pre-signed documents go with it. The homeowner signs a successor-contractor authorization as an addendum at the point of sale, and the installer signs a step-in consent. A written trigger (insolvency, license suspension, or 60 days of no activity) releases the pack to a designated successor. The lender's funding portal requires a complete pack before releasing M1 or M2, so deposits cannot be skipped. Trigger jobs are cured at a pre-agreed per-AHJ rate card. The cure is paid from the last milestone (M3) the lender still holds on that job, plus a small installer holdback. Lenders also get a continuity score per dealer (record completeness, PTO lag, license and lien status). Homeowners get a 'job protected' certificate that installers can use in sales.
why_now: Freedom Forever's collapse made 'will you still be here at PTO?' the first objection at every kitchen table, and made lenders' dealer-risk teams look for controls beyond credit checks. The 25D end is shrinking installer margins and raising failure odds. Agentic capture and CRM APIs make per-job record collection cheap enough for a $60-100 fee. ABS investors can now cite a specific 2026 case when they ask sponsors about continuity.
revenue_model: Installer pays $60-100 per job (about 0.2-0.3% of a $30-35k job). Lender pays a platform fee of $5-10k a month for dealer continuity scoring and pack access. On a trigger, cure work is billed at $1.5-4k per job plus a $500 PTO bonus, funded from the held M3 milestone. Later: a workmanship warranty backed by the reserve, and a recognized 'backup installer' role in ABS structures. Illustration: 3 pilot installers at 800 jobs each is roughly $145-240k a year in deposit fees before lender fees or cure revenue.
non_obvious_insight: The cure budget already exists. On many dealer-channel loans the final milestone (roughly 10-25% of the loan) is not paid until PTO, so on every stranded job the lender is still holding thousands of dollars that would have gone to the dead installer. The only missing piece is a pre-signed right to spend it. And the escrow has an enforcement mechanism that software-escrow lacked: the lender controls the money, so 'no pack, no milestone payment' means installers deposit because that is how they get paid. The party who needs the protection (the lender) is not the party who pays (the installer), and making escrow a sales badge and a dealer-tier perk closes that gap.
first_30_days: Draft the continuity pack spec and the successor-contractor authorization with a solar or construction attorney. Map contractor-of-record change rules for the 10 largest AHJs and top 2-3 utilities in one metro. Recruit 5 installers through former installer ops people and offer a free 90-day pilot in exchange for the badge. Call 3 lender dealer-risk heads with a one-page pitch: escrowed dealers get faster funding or lower holdbacks, and you get a first-call cure vendor. Target 3 installer LOIs and 1 lender pilot letter by day 30, and first live deposits by day 60. Riskiest assumption to test: will a lender change its funding conditions for a pilot dealer group. Test it with a credit union first.
lineage: mutation of I1175 ('Finish Crew: Stranded Solar Job Completion'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: GreenLancer (Solar Repair / O&M network), Lender in-house step-in (GoodLeap, Sunrun, EverBright, EnFin, Credit Human, Participate, Project Solar; also Dividend Finance), Atma Energy (installer taking over stranded Freedom Forever jobs), Local rescue and completion contractors (Revival Solar, ECG Solar, Optimus Energy Solutions, Advance Solar, Solar Discovery). White space: The unserved wedge is portfolio-level, event-driven triage, not crews. (1) Forensic records recovery at scale. No competitor found sells a forensic pack per stranded loan (AHJ permit file, utility interconnection record, dead installer's CRM and design files, distributor and consignment serials, photo audit) sorted into cure tiers with a cost-to-cure and expected-PTO dashboard across a lender's whole book. GreenLancer and the local rescue firms all work job by job. (2) Servicers, credit unions and ABS trustees without operations. The seven Freedom Forever financiers have ops teams, and Sunrun and GoodLeap have crews. Solar Servicing LLC (which took over Mosaic's servicing), credit unions, bank holders and ABS investors have no step-in playbook. I found no completion vendor aimed at them. Lenders may not know which loans sit on de-energized systems, so an identify-then-cure offer has little competition. (4) Standby retainer plus pre-negotiated per-AHJ and per-utility contractor-of-record transfer playbooks for the next failure. Not white space: the first-wave Freedom Forever completion work. The stay-relief order dates to about August 2026, so the seven named financiers have probably already picked contractors, and GreenLancer says it already serves seven financiers. | How this version avoids them: GreenLancer, local rescue contractors and Atma all start after failure, job by job, for an already-staffed lender. This owns the pre-failure moment, sits inside the dealer agreement and the installer's workflow, and earns recurring per-job revenue from installers. When a trigger fires, the company is first-called under a pre-signed rate card and can subcontract to GreenLancer-style shops or local firms. Lender in-house step-in desks have no installer-side records capture, and installers work with 3-5 lenders and will not deposit into five separate lender portals, so neutral multi-lender escrow wins. Solar Insure and OhmSnap serve owners after bankruptcy, and Enphase's program is post-PTO. Main risk is a big lender building a proprietary version, which the neutral multi-lender position is meant to counter.

title: Warranty Desk Embedded in Maintenance Software
one_liner: A white-label, success-fee warranty desk sold through mid-tier maintenance-tracking and MRO software vendors. The removal event, the PO and the repair invoice meet inside a system the operator already uses, and the software vendor earns a revenue share.
customer: The channel buyer is the partnerships or customer-success head at a mid-tier maintenance-tracking or MRO software vendor with 50-400 operator customers. The payer is the operator on that software: a regional airline, Part 135 or cargo-feeder fleet, or helicopter operator. The vendor pays nothing. It receives 30% of our fee and gets a renewal and differentiation story.
problem: Operators on these systems already hold structured removal, install, hours and cycles data, plus POs and receiving records. That is the data-access problem the parent idea could not solve. Still, warranty stays unclaimed, because the missing pieces are things software does not do. Someone has to read negotiated PDF terms, file on each shop's own template, and chase the shop for 60-90 days. Vendors cannot staff claims specialists. Operators' thin materials teams cannot absorb the work. The claim is decided at the removal moment, when a technician pulls a unit at 3 AM and nobody sees the terms. Only the maintenance software sees that event.
solution: The vendor gives a read-only export or API for removals, installs, POs and receiving. We load each shop's warranty terms from the operator's contracts and invoice PDFs. When a technician posts a removal against a serialized component, we return a lookup card in seconds, inside the vendor's UI or by email or Slack in the first version. The card shows who repaired the unit and when, the remaining window in days, hours or cycles, the evidence checklist, and a pre-drafted claim. Our claims specialists then file, chase and post the credit memo back into the system as a warranty record. A monthly sweep catches misses, late turn times, no-fault-found fees and open cores. Operators sign a contingency agreement. The vendor contract is non-exclusive and revenue-share only.
why_now: LLM extraction of warranty fine print and invoice PDFs means one specialist can now run claims for dozens of operators. Software vendors are also under pressure to prove value in the renewals of small and mid-size operators. Ramco advertises warranty-recovery savings, which shows the outcome is being marketed. Nobody sells the outcome as a service to the other vendors.
revenue_model: Operators pay 20% of cash and credits recovered, with a 12-month tail. The vendor gets 30% of our fee, about 6 points of recoveries, and owns the relationship. From year 2, vendors can bundle a Warranty Desk line item at $1-2k/month per operator, with us as wholesale fulfillment at about $600/month plus the success fee. Aggregated vendor-level claim data is a later product.
non_obvious_insight: Maintenance software has an adoption problem, not a feature problem. Warranty fields and modules sit empty because filling them takes human work: reading PDFs and chasing vendors. A managed service that makes the module produce cash is worth more to a vendor than building the feature. The vendor also supplies what our own sales cycle lacks: structured removal data, a warm introduction, and a trigger at the exact moment the claim is won or lost. Vendors will not build claim-chasing themselves. Terms are negotiated PDFs, and staffing claims desks is not a software margin.
first_30_days: Approach 8 mid-tier software vendors' partnership heads with a one-page offer: we make a slice of your customers' warranty tracking pay, with no cost to you and 30% of our fee. Ask each for 2-3 design-partner operators. Work as a concierge service, with no integration yet. The operator exports removals, POs and receiving from the software's standard CSV export, we match against invoice PDFs, and we deliver a ranked claim list with the vendor's customer-success manager on the call. Build the removal lookup as a simple web form or email responder. Sign a revenue-share MOU with the first vendor and aim for the first credit memo by day 30-45. Hire a retired materials coordinator for shop quirks. Success is 2 operators with live removal-time lookups by month 3.
lineage: mutation of I0195 ('Contingency Recovery of Missed Rotable Repair Warranties'), type: new-customer-or-model
